Title: Environment: A giant logger and a tiny bird test limits of conservation law
Text: About two years ago, some Pacific Lumber Co. employees spotted what looked like a tiny marbled murrelet -- a protected seabird that's snarling the company's logging efforts -- right in executive Thomas Herman's living room.    It turned out to be a picture, affixed to a dart board for a company party hosted by Mr. Herman, who is responsible for Pacific Lumber's logging operations. Employees spent the evening throwing darts at the target.    Mr. Herman says the episode didn't reflect "any hatred of the species." But critics wonder. And they cite it and other disclosures that have emerged from a closely watched case pending in San Francisco federal court that pits Pacific Lumber, the world's largest producer of redwood lumber, against advocates for the murrelet, which is under federal and state protection. At issue is whether Pacific Lumber may log 137 acres of company-owned, ancient forest in Owl Creek, one of the largest intact stands of privately owned virgin redwoods -- and some of the last marbled murrelet habitat, biologists say.    The case is a key legal test of how far regulators can go to enforce the federal Endangered Species Act on private land. Earlier this year, a federal appeals court in Washington, D.C., ruled in a case known as Sweet Home that, contrary to what was assumed, the government has very limited power to enforce restrictions on private property to protect wildlife under the act. Now loggers, miners and other landowners are trying to get the country's courts to apply the ruling in other conservation cases.    Property-rights advocates hail Sweet Home as blessed relief from government regulation, but environmentalists fear it could be a devastating blow to wildlife protection. "If Sweet Home becomes the standard, it would be extremely damaging to our ability to prevent extinctions," says Suellen Lowry, a lawyer for the Sierra Club Legal Defense Fund.    The Pacific Lumber case, expected to be decided this month by Judge Louis C. Bechtle, was filed before the Sweet Home decision. But Pacific Lumber is using it as its principal defense, and the case will be the first test of how courts will apply it in other situations.    The Owl Creek showdown dates to 1990, when Pacific Lumber first proposed logging in the grove. Objections from environmentalists and regulators stalled the plan, but eventually, the state approved it, with conditions. The main one was that Pacific Lumber cooperate with regulators to minimize harm to murrelets.    But over a weekend in June 1992, Pacific Lumber cut down dozens of ancient trees in Owl Creek before regulators found out and stopped it. State and federal regulators say Pacific Lumber then promised not to log there again until the two camps agreed on a murrelet-protection plan. Then Pacific Lumber cut more Owl Creek redwoods over Thanksgiving, when regulators were on vacation.    Pacific Lumber maintains it had every right to log in Owl Creek because it had fulfilled its agreement to "cooperate" with regulators and because its logging plan had been approved by the state. But regulators didn't see it that way, and furious environmentalists sued. They accuse Pacific Lumber of violating the Endangered Species Act by destroying murrelet habitat and seek to block logging in the grove. If logging is permitted, the bird "will be pushed even closer to the brink of extinction," says Mark P. Harris, an attorney for the plaintiffs.    In court, Pacific Lumber attorney Alson Kemp called such arguments "piddly." The company questions whether murrelets should be protected in California, in part because they're so uncommon. "So little is known about murrelets that the government can't say with any certainty whether logging would threaten them or not," Mr. Kemp contends.    Biologists didn't discover until 1974 that the murrelet nests only in coastal forests in California, Oregon, Washington and Alaska. Only 71 nests have been found. The bird flies at up to 60 miles per hour and only at night, making it hard to detect.    The Endangered Species Act prohibits "taking" of protected species, defined two ways: outright killing or "habitat modification" that so disturbs a species's territory that its population is likely to be harmed. The Sweet Home judges said that, on public land, regulators may prevent both types of take. On private land, the judges held, regulators can't restrict habitat modification unless it directly and immediately kills an endangered species -- even if the animal might later be harmed.    Pacific Lumber argues that the Sweet Home ruling means it can log its Owl Creek lands because it doesn't expect to kill any murrelets directly. Although biologists dispute that assertion, some private-property-law experts think the company has some strong legal points.    But its case may have been clouded by disclosures about some of its practices. Pacific Lumber's top logging manager, Ray Miller, conceded on the stand that its murrelet surveyors -- who are supposed to scour proposed logging lands for signs of the birds and report to regulators -- were under orders not to record certain evidence used to determine logging restrictions.    For example, surveyors are supposed to inform regulators if they hear a murrelet's distinctive "keer" call. Mr. Miller and several Pacific Lumber surveyors said the company decided, without consulting regulators, that it wouldn't count keer calls as murrelet evidence. Mr. Miller also testified that he once lost a report in which a company wildlife surveyor recorded having heard murrelet wing beats, which regulators consider prime evidence of the birds. In court, Mr. Miller said he replaced the report with one he filled out himself that didn't mention wing beats.    Mike Penny, a Pacific Lumber surveyor, testified that company managers recently "grilled" him when he reported murrelet sightings. He testified a supervisor warned him that "a lot of money was tied up" in Owl Creek and suggested that surveyors' jobs might be at stake if the sighting was reported. The report wasn't altered.    Mary Bullwinkel, a Pacific Lumber spokeswoman, says the company hasn't violated any laws in Owl Creek and defends its murrelet practices. She says keer calls weren't counted as murrelet evidence because the regulators' prescriptions for what constitutes such evidence aren't binding and that the company's murrelet experts considered the calls an unreliable indicator. She says Mr. Miller replaced the report because he had determined that the surveyor wasn't "absolutely, 100%" sure the sounds he detected were wing beats. And she says managers were merely striving to confirm what murrelet activity Mr. Penny had detected.    Whichever way Judge Bechtle rules, it will immediately affect Pacific Lumber, a unit of Maxxam Inc., which is controlled by Texas financier Charles Hurwitz. It is feuding with regulators over a logging plan for Allen Creek, an ancient redwood grove near Owl Creek. Regulators have pronounced Pacific Lumber's murrelet plan inadequate there, too.    (See related letter: "Letters to the Editor: Very Expensive Bird Watching" -- WSJ Nov. 21, 1994)    941020-0117    YY94 MM11  Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: U.S. News: Emperor Penguins to Be Listed As Threatened Species by U.S.
Text: The emperor penguin will soon be considered a threatened species under the Endangered Species Act, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service said. The federal agency said Tuesday it had finalized protections for the species, following a proposal last year. It cited the effects of a warming climate on the sea-ice habitat in Antarctica, where emperor penguins spend the majority of their lives, as the "primary threat to the penguin." "Climate change is having a profound impact on species around the world and addressing it is a priority for the Administration," Fish and Wildlife Service Director Martha Williams said in a statement. "The listing of the emperor penguin serves as an alarm bell but also a call to action." Emperor penguins are considered a bellwether of any future climate changes in Antarctica because their icy habitat is so sensitive to rising temperatures. The current emperor penguin population, estimated to be around 625,000-650,000 individual birds or 270,000-280,000 breeding pairs, appears stable at the moment, according to Fish and Wildlife Service officials. But, they added, "the species is in danger of extinction in the foreseeable future in a significant portion of its range." By 2050, the population is estimated to decrease by 26% to 47%, depending on the level of carbon emissions, Fish and Wildlife Service officials said. "While this estimated decline is concerning, listing the emperor penguin as threatened under the ESA comes while there is still time to prevent the species from extinction," the Fish and Wildlife Service said. The agency's final rule listing the species as threatened will publish Wednesday and go into effect 30 days later. The Endangered Species Act of 1973 can provide benefits to an animal even if it doesn't exist within U.S. borders. The act will usually prohibit the import or export of the animal, as well as its use in interstate commerce and foreign commerce. Listing a species can create increased awareness of the threatened species and provide limited financial assistance to help conservation efforts for species listed in foreign countries. The emperor penguin is the tallest and heaviest of all living penguin species, with adults that can weigh up to 88 pounds. The flightless bird relies on sea ice to forage for food, form breeding colonies and avoid predators. Credit: By Talal Ansari

story: The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service has finalized the listing of the emperor penguin as a threatened species due to the primary threat of climate change affecting its sea-ice habitat in Antarctica. This decision is a response to the alarming decline projected in the penguin population by 2050, which could decrease by 26% to 47% based on carbon emissions levels. The agency emphasizes that while the current population appears stable, the species is in danger of extinction in the foreseeable future, and the listing serves as both a warning and a call to action for conservation efforts.
moral: The Endangered Species Act should be utilized proactively to protect species like the emperor penguin, as timely action can prevent extinction and promote awareness and conservation efforts.

Title: Washington Tries Board System To Handle Water-Rights Issues
Text: When James Holmes, owner of Ceil Du Cheval Vineyard in West Richland, Wash., decided to plant more of his prize-winning merlot grapes and irrigate them with water from a well on the property, he needed permission. So he asked the Benton County Water Conservancy Board for a change in his water-rights permit. Mr. Holmes applied for authorization to irrigate 20 additional acres, pledging to use a new drip method that wouldn't draw any more from the well than the vineyard's outdated sprinkler system had. He received the go-ahead within six months. If Ceil Du Cheval (French for horse heaven) had pressed its case directly with the Washington Department of Ecology, as Mr. Holmes initially planned, rather than through the one-year-old conservancy board, he believes he would still be waiting for an answer. "It would have taken forever," he says. "I'd be dead before it happened." Even department officials don't argue with his assessment. With demand for water growing and supply increasingly restricted by the Endangered Species Act -- and with the agency chronically under-funded -- the queue of candidates for permit adjustments and new water rights is 6,800 applicants long. The notorious backlog prompted the Washington Legislature in 1997 to pass a law authorizing a network of conservancy boards, which lawmakers reckoned would ease the gridlock and give locals some say over the allocation of natural resources. The emergence of the boards -- along with individuals who act as "water brokers" in the state -- underscores a broader trend in water rights: Residents and developers are increasingly seeking alternatives to finding water since getting new rights directly from the state is next to impossible. And it's unlikely to become any easier; with Washington's population projected to increase by about 14% over the next decade, it will no doubt give rise to an ever-greater number of disputes over the water supply. Later this week, on Dec. 18, the Department of Ecology is scheduled to implement the final regulations necessary to set up three-member boards in any of the 39 counties in the state that petitions for one. And by the middle of next year, at least a dozen are expected to be in business. "The future lies in making better use of existing water, because there is less and less opportunity to establish new rights," says Fred Rajala, a water-resource specialist with the ecology agency in Olympia. Not everyone, however, is enthusiastic. Some environmentalists are unhappy with what they view as the inexperience of board members, who are appointed by county commissioners. "We think the boards are packed with a bunch of lay people who have little to no experience with water management and are riddled with conflicts of interest," says Rob Caldwell, director of the Seattle-based Center for Environmental Law & Policy. Mr. Caldwell is worried that as the boards proliferate, they'll be used by developers to bypass stricter state environmental standards. That, he says, violates the Legislature's intent -- and could put at risk the flows of rivers and streams that support threatened and endangered species of fish. Mr. Caldwell says the center believes the Department of Ecology will be overstepping its authority if it implements regulations regarding the boards this week. Tribal leaders also worry about the conservancy boards. Steve Suagee, a lawyer for the Colville Tribes in eastern Washington, says the boards pose "major problems." Mr. Suago says while he supports local control in theory, he is concerned that board members aren't familiar with federal laws that deal with tribal rights and so might "disregard" those legal protections. Rep. Gary Chandler, a Moses Lake Republican who sponsored the 1997 legislation and is now co-chairman of the House Agriculture and Ecology Committee, says he isn't surprised by the objections. "When haven't the environmentalists filed some suit to block something like this?" he says. But when the boards are finally up and running, Rep. Chandler says, "they'll give a lot of relief to the department of ecology. They should have gone forward two years ago, when the bill passed." In Benton County, board members -- Daryll Olsen, an irrigation consultant with a doctorate in applied-energy studies; John Jaksch, who has a doctorate in resource economics; and Matt Berg, an agricultural economist -- take offense at the center's contentions. "Water-conservancy boards are a reflection of legislation that is the most progressive when it comes to water marketing in the western United States," says Mr. Olsen, the board's chairman. He adds: "If the environmentalists had a good case, they would have appealed our decisions, and they didn't." The conservancy-board experiment is new. Only five are fully operational, and together they have so far made just seven water-rights decisions, which must be approved by the Department of Ecology. Decisions can be appealed to the Pollution Control Hearings Board by any interested party. Henry Johnson, a former farmer and property manager who is chairman of the Franklin County Water Conservancy Board in Pasco, concedes that the required training for board members -- 32 hours of schooling by DOE staffers on issues of law and hydrology -- isn't much. "I certainly wouldn't characterize it as rigorous," Mr. Johnson says. But he notes that most members have experience in the field. And, he adds, when compared with the alternative, the conservancy-board system will serve a critical need given the impasse at the state level. "I think that they're going to gain prominence quickly," he says. "When people become familiar with what we're empowered to do and the relative speed with which we can act compared to DOE, people will find a lot of relief in dealing with us." The Department of Ecology has been strapped for cash for since 1994 when the Legislature didn't approve continued funding for the water-resources division, resulting in a 60% budget cut and a total loss of 46 positions. The Legislature approved four new staff positions for ecology in 1999. As the agency has struggled to keep up with applications, the implementation of the Endangered Species Act has begun to curb government's ability to meet the public's demand for water. Fifteen runs of salmon are listed as either endangered or threatened in Washington, along with many other species of fish and wildlife. Federally mandated preservation plans only now being devised -- and legal action by environmentalists -- are certain to make the business of apportioning water resources even more difficult. For that reason, developers and business interests are generally supportive of the conservancy-board system. "It's the only glimmer of hope we have to get through this horrible backlog," says Jody Slavik, legal counsel for the Building Industry Association of Washington in Olympia. "He who controls the water controls everything, particularly growth in our state. That's why the environmentalists are against this. ...They're short-sighted and want to stop everything." The availability of water is definitely a key selling point for real-estate agents, according to Tim Reierson, a former water-rights investigator for the Department of Ecology and now a water consultant in Yakima. "I have my ears open all the time for potential water rights that can be marketed and clients looking for water rights," Mr. Reierson says. "The boards bring on an extra work force to deal with the changes that are out there." Joe Mentor, a Seattle lawyer who has brokered several water-rights sales, agrees, calling transfers "the wave of the future." Mr. Mentor and brokers like him can't change waters rights; only the Department of Ecology and the boards, and in some cases the courts, can do that. But private middlemen can -- and increasingly do -- act as go-betweens for rights-holders eager to sell and developers eager for water. Mr. Mentor, for example, recently purchased from seven farmers and other landowners enough rights to supply most of the water necessary for Trend West, a resort being built near Roslyn. Such transfers don't bother most environmentalists, since existing rights move from those who don't need them to those who do, making for an efficient distribution of a limited resource. What they object to is what happens in cases such as that of Ceil Du Cheval Vineyard, in which the Benton County board allowed Mr. Holmes's right to be altered without, the environmentalists complain, the proper analysis by trained technical personnel of its impact on fish. Locals board don't have paid staff. Moreover, says Mr. Caldwell of the law and policy center in Seattle, Mr. Holmes's needs weren't serious enough for him to enjoy such a swift and positive response. "If you get a water user that just wants to maximize water use, like spreading it further in the case of the winery, there's no direct benefit to society," Mr. Caldwell says. "No benefit isn't good enough to give them a priority to change their water right. They should stand in line with everyone else." Standing in line, of course, is what lawmakers said they wanted to help Washingtonians avoid when they passed the legislation sanctioning local boards. For his part, Mr. Holmes certainly disagrees with Mr. Caldwell's assessment. Mr. Holmes initially applied to the department for permission to modify his rights in early 1997, before the Benton County panel existed, and says he got nowhere. Now, he's a fan of conservancy boards. "When you change water from one place to another, it's a pretty simple thing," he says. "And there's only one question: Does it hurt anyone? It's a very local issue, and it should be decided on a one-page application." Evidence is abundant, most observers say, that the old way of doing water business in Washington simply doesn't work anymore. Just last week, citing its inability to win the water rights it needed, Seattle-based R.D. Merrill Co. threw in the towel after spending some $20 million on plans for Arrowleaf Resort and the Freestone Inn in the Methow Valley, a resort that was to include a golf course, a 100-room lodge, 565 single-family units, 20 miles of hiking trails and an equestrian center. With 40 applicants in the queue ahead of Merrill, and two runs of fish in the area protected by the Endangered Species Act, the company figured there was no end in sight. If there had been a conservancy board in Okanogan County, says Tom Bartholomew, Arrowleaf's project manager, "that absolutely could have helped. But there wasn't one." Mary Getchell, a spokeswoman for the department, says the chances Arrowleaf would have been granted new water rights were slim; developers are better off asking conservancy boards for transfers, or making deals through water brokers, she and others say. "There's just not a lot of water available," Ms. Getchell says. "The game is changing." Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: The Morning Brief: How Long and How Far Will Oil Prices Decline?
Text: The Wall Street Journal Online The Morning Brief, a look at the day's biggest news, is emailed to subscribers by 7 a.m. every business day. Sign up for the e-mail here. Crude futures continue to slide even as war rages near a Caspian pipeline, leaving little doubt that the near-term direction of oil prices is down. But the longer-term outlook is less clear, and depends in part on whether we have permanently altered our energy-consuming habits. Yesterday, benchmark crude oil on the Nymex fell to as low as $112.72 a barrel before settling at $114.45 a barrel, down 75 cents. Since June 30, the price of oil has fallen 18%, The Wall Street Journal reports. The newspaper says the rapid decline reflects pessimism about demand from Europe and Japan as those two economies continue to soften. "Inside the commodity-trading pits and brokerage houses, the conversation isn't whether prices are pulling back in the near term, but how far and for how long," the Journal writes. Other factors contributing to lower oil prices are the stronger dollar, which makes commodities more expensive to purchase with other currencies, and diminished demand from China, the Los Angeles Times reports. In July, Chinese oil imports fell 7% to a seven-month low, according to Beijing, and the Times says that could reflect factory closures as the country tried to cut down on pollution ahead of the Olympics. Americans, meanwhile, are curbing what the Journal calls our "legendary appetite for energy" by buying smaller cars and more efficient appliances, driving less and more slowly, using less packaging, changing distribution networks, and choosing locally made products. Consumers stung by surges in oil and gas prices have resolved not to count on cheap energy any longer, analysts tell BusinessWeek. "The changes we're seeing are permanent," Fadel Gheit, senior oil analyst for Oppenheimer Holdings, tells the magazine. "People are not going to rush to the dealer to buy Hummers again. The energy shock was beneficial in the longer term to our psychology." Not all observers agree. Auto-data tracker Edmunds.com says that, as prices have fallen at the gas pump, interest in smaller vehicles is beginning to level off, and consideration of gas-electric hybrids is down 34% since June, according to the L.A. Times. Still, the Journal notes, lasting declines in oil prices are less likely than they once were, given the rapidly growing economies of China and India. Despite the recent decline in the market, prices remain above the prior inflation-adjusted peak of $106.15, set in April 1980. And this morning in its monthly oil-market report, the International Energy Agency said the tight balance of global supply and demand for oil is easing, but warned that conditions may again tighten in coming months due to healthy consumption in China and geopolitical factors, as Dow Jones Newswires reports. The recent decline in oil prices despite the conflict between oil- producer Russia and what the Journal calls the "oil crossroads of Georgia" reignited debate in some quarters about the extent to which speculation has played a role in recent oil-price volatility. "It speaks volumes about how this market was hijacked by investors who pushed the market up -- and now they are pushing it down," Peter Beutel, president of energy risk-management firm Cameron Hanover, tells the L.A. Times. Indeed, the Washington Post, citing Wall Street brokers and congressional investigators, reports that sovereign-wealth funds "are now among the biggest speculators in the trading of oil and other vital goods like corn and cotton in the United States." The paper writes that the activity is going undetected by the market's regulator, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, because the funds invest through brokers known as "swap dealers" who often operate on unregulated markets. And the Journal writes that noncommercial oil traders such as hedge funds have taken on an increasingly bearish view of oil -- perhaps in part because the credit crunch has made it more difficult to meet margin calls to support bullish positions. --- The Role of Oil in the Georgian Conflict. . . Oil, it seems, is one issue at the heart of the violent conflict between Russia and Georgia. In striking its neighbor hard in the ostensible tussle to control the breakaway Georgian province of South Ossetia, Moscow is signaling that it won't give up control of the oil- rich Caspian region, the Financial Times reports. "Georgia has scant energy resources of its own but hosts pipelines built by international oil majors to carry Caspian oil and gas to western markets," the newspaper writes. "The so-called east-west energy corridor across Azerbaijan and Georgia to Turkey, established with strong political backing from the U.S., has eroded Russia's stranglehold over energy exports from one of the world's few remaining untapped oil provinces." Analysts tell BusinessWeek that Moscow must walk a fine line between cementing its dominance of European energy supplies and not spooking Europeans into backing the construction of yet more non-Russian pipelines, but that any expansion of European or U.S. influence is unlikely since no Caspian leader will want to put his survival on the line by embracing a new Western project. Chris Ruppel, an energy analyst at Greenwich brokerage Execution, tells the magazine, "Russia has demonstrated that its military is a force to reckon with, that it can defeat a Western-trained force, and that the West and NATO will not act to intervene." It remains to be seen whether Europe is wholly without influence. This morning, just before French President Nicolas Sarkozy arrived at the Kremlin to negotiate a European Union-backed truce, Russian President Dmitri Medvedev took to the airwaves to announce that Russia would end its current military operation against Georgian forces because it has achieved its goals, as The Wall Street Journal reports. But Mr. Medvedev stopped short of saying Russia would withdraw its troops from Georgia, and even as his comments were broadcast, Agence France-Presse cited a Georgian official as saying the Russian air force had attacked the key Baku-Tblisi-Ceyhan pipeline. "We don't know yet whether it was damaged. It's a second attempt to bomb this pipeline since Aug. 10," Alexander Lomaia, secretary of Georgia's National Security Council, told AFP. --- . . . And the Conflict's Role in U.S. Policy The flow of oil and gas revenue is also at the heart of a "troubling strategic reality" which will confront either Republican Sen. John McCain or Democratic Sen. Barack Obama when November's election winner assumes the White House, as Wall Street Journal columnist Gerald F. Seib says. Just as funds from the sale of expensive oil have emboldened Moscow to defy the U.S. by attacking Georgia, "The rise of energy prices also is enriching other bad actors, creating a kind of globe-girdling string of well-heeled regional antagonists the U.S. can't ignore," Mr. Seib writes, citing Iran's push to build a nuclear program and bankroll militias like Hamas and Hezbollah, and Venezuela's antagonism toward America. The next president will need to build stronger ties to Mexico, Chile and Brazil to offset Venezuela's influence, Mr. Seib writes, and will want to cultivate ties with China to avoid having similar problems with Beijing that the U.S. will apparently have with Moscow. Leading up to November, the escalation in the Caspian "has put a new focus on the increasingly hard line that Senator John McCain has taken against Russia in recent years, with stances that have often gone well beyond those of the Bush administration and its focus on engagement," the New York Times writes. Sen. McCain has befriended Georgian President Mikheil Saakashvili and embraced the country's efforts to join NATO, and has called for excluding Russia from the Group of Eight leading industrialized nations. In contrast, Sen. Obama has made clear he favors more engagement with Russia, but, the Times notes, this week the two rivals found themselves holding more or less the same position, calling for a U.N. resolution on the violence, for a path to NATO membership for Georgia, and deployment of an international peacekeeping force. --- Also of Note. . . Financial Times: J.P. Morgan Chase provided evidence of more turbulence in financial markets, warning that stormy credit conditions had forced it to take a $1.5 billion write-down on mortgage-backed assets in July. In a regulatory filing, J.P. Morgan said since the beginning of July, trading conditions in the mortgage market "had substantially deteriorated." Wall Street Journal: Securities regulators are widening the list of Wall Street firms that are being told to fix the auction-rate securities mess. Morgan Stanley was the latest to act in response, saying it would buy back about $4.5 billion in securities it sold to retail clients, charities and small businesses. The action came after New York Attorney General Andrew Cuomo's office sent letters to Morgan Stanley, J.P. Morgan Chase and Wachovia, demanding they make their investors whole for auction-rate securities that were sold to them. Dow Jones Newswires: UBS said it will begin separating its troubled investment bank from its money-management arm for the wealthy, as mortgage losses continued to hammer the beleaguered Swiss bank in the second quarter. Bowing to shareholder pressure, the Zurich-based bank said its main units will be separated, backing away from its integrated model, but said it has no specific plans to sell its investment bank, the source of major losses. CNET: Advanced Micro Devices announced its most powerful graphics technology to date, going after Nvidia in the rarified -- and closely watched --enthusiast game segment. This also marks the current performance pinnacle of AMD's strategy to beat Nvidia at the high end by building comparatively smaller chips and then ganging them together for better performance. Associated Press: A roadside bomb hit a Pakistan air force truck in a northwestern city today, killing about 12 people as the military pounded insurgent positions in a nearby tribal region. Interior Ministry chief Rehman Malik said al Qaeda-linked militants were likely behind the attack. Separately, Northwest Pakistan lawmakers have passed a resolution against President Pervez Musharraf, the second major act in the ruling coalition's campaign to impeach and oust the embattled leader. Times-Picayune: Federal investigators collected documents from the shuttered New Orleans Affordable Homeownership Corp., the city- chartered and city-financed nonprofit that ran a home-remediation program in 2006 and 2007. The city nonprofit has been under scrutiny as news reports raised questions about whether its contractors billed taxpayers for work they didn't perform on blighted New Orleans homes. The remediation program, aimed at the poor and elderly, was touted as a salve to sagging neighborhoods by Mayor Ray Nagin in his 2007 budget address. Washington Post: The Bush administration proposed a regulatory overhaul of the Endangered Species Act to allow federal agencies to decide whether protected species would be imperiled by agency projects, eliminating the independent scientific reviews that have been required for more than three decades. The new rules, which will be subject to a 30-day per comment period, would use administrative powers to make broad changes in the law that Congress has resisted for years. CBS: Some people say you can't outrun time, but a new study has found that pounding the pavement might slow down the aging clock. Researchers from Stanford University say older runners have fewer disabilities and a long lifespan compared to their non-running peers. They tracked runners for more than 20 years and found elderly runners had a more active lifestyle and were less likely to die early. --- Quote of the Day "I train to win on my worst day," Aaron Peirsol told ESPN after taking a gold medal for the U.S. in the 100-meter backstroke this morning at the Water Cube in Beijing. "Honestly, I don't know what goes on in these other guys' heads. I know what I have to do to get my hand on the wall." --- Write to Elana Beiser at elana.beiser@wsj.com --- Some links in this column are to sites that require a subscription or registration.

Title: U.S. News: Yellowstone Grizzlies to Lose Protections
Text: The Trump administration said it will removeendangered-species protections for the Yellowstone grizzly bear, a move that was initiated bythe Obama administration after the numbers of the West's largest land predator rebounded sharply over the past four decades. The decision, criticized by environmentalists, paves the way for grizzly-hunting to resume in some places after a 40-year ban. Grizzly bears in and around Yellowstone National Park had plummeted to as few as 136 by 1975, when they were listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act. Because of aban on hunting and other protections, the number of grizzlies in a Greater Yellowstone ecosystem that includes parts of Idaho, Montana and Wyoming has increased more than fivefold to an estimated 700,according to the Interior Department. The federal government aimed to boost the population to 500 grizzlies. The animal can weigh up to 600 pounds. Interior Secretary Ryan Zinke, a former Montana congressman who announced the delistingThursday, hailed the recovery as one of the nation's greatest conservation success stories. "As a kid who grew up in Montana, I can tell you that this is a long time coming and very good news for many communities and advocates in the Yellowstone region," Mr. Zinke said in a statement. Environmental groups condemned the move and vowed to try to fight it in the courts. Lawsuits filed by environmentalists succeeded in blocking efforts by the Bush administration to delist the grizzly in 2007, when their numbers already were considered recovered by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. Environmentalists saygrizzlies have a slow reproduction rate and would be imperiled as a result of hunting and other dangers. Once the rule by the Fish and Wildlife Service takes effect laterthis year, states will regain their authority to resume trophy hunts that have been banned for 40 years. The grizzlies would remain protected from hunting in Yellowstone and Grand Teton national parks. "This premature decision to remove endangered-species protections could set grizzly recovery back by decades," said Michael Brune, executive director of the Sierra Club, in a statement. "The end result will be fewer bears restricted to an even smaller area," Mr. Brune said. Supporters of the delisting, though, say there are so many Yellowstone grizzlies that conflicts with humans have increased, as well as attacks on livestock. "Grizzly bears have met or exceeded recovery objectives since 2003 and have long warranted delisting," Wyoming Republican Gov. Matt Mead said in a statement. The Wyoming governor, among other Westerners, asked the Obama administration to resume the delisting process. In 2016, the Fish and Wildlife Service issued a draft notice to take the bears off the list, as states including Wyoming gave assurances they would continue to manage the grizzlies so their numbers remained healthy. The debate over grizzlies is reminiscent of the one over the gray wolf, another iconic predator that was reintroduced to Yellowstone in 1995 under endangered-species protection. But as the number of wolves exploded, they were delisted in both Idaho and Montana.   Credit: By Jim Carlton
event: removal of endangered-species protections for the Yellowstone grizzly bear
story: The Trump administration announced the delisting of the Yellowstone grizzly bear, a decision that follows a significant population rebound due to protections under the Endangered Species Act. This action, criticized by environmentalists, allows for the resumption of grizzly hunting after a 40-year ban, despite concerns about the species' slow reproduction rate and potential risks from hunting. Supporters argue that the population has exceeded recovery goals, while opponents fear that this decision could jeopardize the species' future.

Title: REVIEW & OUTLOOK (Editorial): Burying the Future
Text: A federal judge has plopped another science and technology choice in the lap of the Clinton administration. As with the Von Roll incinerator debate in Ohio, this one concerns disposal, but it directly affects medicine and biotechnology, industries on which the new President can help the United States build a higher-wage economy. In a taste of what awaits other parts of the country, California's biomedical and surgical talent at work in the field of nuclear medicine is running up against a desperate scarcity of sites for discarding the remnants of low-level nuclear technology used in so many cutting-edge fields of research and practice. The situation became pressing this year when two Western U.S. dumps became off-limits to California shipments, forcing them to a remaining destination in South Carolina until that, too, becomes unavailable over the next couple of years. Governor Pete Wilson, fighting a many-front war to keep industry from leaving his reeling state, stepped up efforts to open a California site, as was promised years ago to the affected scientists and entrepreneurs, and as the federal government itself has demanded of it (and other states). He wanted to swap for a federally owned parcel in the Southern California desert, outside the desolate town of Needles. But the state Lands Commission, controlled by Mr. Wilson's partisan foes, blocked the exchange. So he cooked up a deal with departing Interior Secretary Manuel Lujan to sell the site for a sum to be provided by U.S. Ecology, the company that would operate the landfill. The usual environmentalist and NIMBY howls have accompanied the whole process, with objections centering on the potential for radioactive leakage through an aquifer to the Colorado River about 13 miles away. It looked, however, as if the project at least would be moved a big step forward. Then came Tuesday's ruling by District Judge Marilyn Patel in San Francisco. Judge Patel, a familiar name to those who follow bench writs, invoked a different basis: the Endangered Species Act. (Desert tortoises, you see.) The judge's injunction has put over the federal sale to Bruce Babbitt's reign at Interior. Probably Vice President Gore and the greenies will want to weigh in. For the sake of balance, Hazel O'Leary at Energy ought to have a say. She seems to recognize that impeding commerce in the name of all that is good and pure sometimes has adverse effects on real people. Some opponents charge that biotech is a cover for using the site to contain the "hot" remains of decommissioned nuclear plants. Presumably public officials would be held accountable for observing whatever conditions are laid down at the time a site is opened. Moreover, from the intensity with which the scientific-business sector has supported this siting, they would appear not to think their interests can be met in another way. Without Ward Valley, "nuclear waste" is going to have to make a trek of 3,000 miles, or collect on the premises of California's labs and hospitals, most of which are near residential neighborhoods. If the threat posed by these materials is anything like what the alarmists say, those two options would seem to be especially unpleasant alternatives. A final option, and one that those who use nuclear technology will come to eventually in any case, is to move their facilities to wherever disposal can be arranged, or simply shut down operations that promise life-saving medicine as well as high-value occupations. That is not what Governor Wilson wants in California, and it is not what President Clinton must seek for the nation.

Title: Hydroelectric Dams Generate a Flood of Controversy
Text: POTLATCH, Wash. -- When the two-dam complex known as the Cushman Project took shape 70 years ago, promotion of hydroelectric power was a major federal policy. Before a crowd of admiring school children, President Coolidge flipped a switch in the White House, opening floodgates here to start Cushman's mighty turbines whirling.    Built by the city of Tacoma, Wash., the dams' cheap, clean electricity ended chaotic brownouts. They also meant more jobs and new industries that Tacoma lured to enjoy what it called America's "Electric City."    Those turbines still spin, generating about 20% of the city's power. But for hydroelectric dams, the political world has turned upside down. The Cushman Project is under fire from environmental groups and more than a dozen state and federal agencies over allegations ranging from harming the region's wildlife to damaging the culture of a nearby Indian tribe. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission deliberated the issues for 24 years. Last year, it decreed that Cushman may have a new license to operate but only after adopting expensive fish-protecting measures that the city says would result in an annual $2.5 million loss for the project.    Today's federal policy puts the future of scores of such dams in doubt. In place of President Coolidge, there is Bruce Babbitt, secretary of the Interior Department, who has begun taking a sledgehammer to various dams deemed no longer useable, giving them a televised tap before the wrecking crews arrive. In his dam-busting forays, which often leave the dams replaced by fast-running rivers, Mr. Babbitt has said he senses a "deep, widespread understanding that Americans overshot the mark in our dam-building frenzy." Mr. Babbitt celebrated another dam deconstruction yesterday, saying that PacifiCorp's decision to tear down a small hydroelectric dam on the White Salmon River in Washington state was an "excellent outcome."    The Cushman case, which Tacoma is taking to the U.S. Court of Appeals in Washington, D.C., "is a real concern for our industry," says Linda Church Ciocci, head of the National Hydropower Association, which represents owners of the nation's hydroelectric dams. "They see it as an indication of where things are going." The economic worth of goods produced by the dams, which include clean electricity, flood control and water for irrigation, she says, are being outweighed in the licensing process by environmental claims.    Within the next 15 years, she says, 284 hydro-dam owners, or roughly two-thirds of those not operated by the federal government, are heading for the same rough FERC relicensing gauntlet. She worries that many projects, burdened with new environmental restrictions like Cushman, won't be able to compete against coal and gas-fired plants.    From an environmental point of view, that might seem odd. Plants powered by fossil fuel create tons of air pollutants including carbon dioxide, which many scientists claim is overheating the Earth's climate by creating an atmosphere that traps more of the sun's heat. Dams, which generate about 11% of the nation's power, emit no air pollutants.    But in the current Rodney Dangerfield climate, that doesn't generate much respect. And the big federal power dams, which aren't regulated by the FERC, face an even tougher gauntlet. Under the U.S. Endangered Species Act, federal agencies that protect wildlife can issue "mandates" requiring the dams to change activities deemed harmful to animals.    That the dams don't produce carbon dioxide doesn't factor into this, explains Brian Gorman, a spokesman for the Commerce Department's National Marine Fisheries Service. "Our obligation is purely a biological one. We will look only at the biology of the fish and only at endangered salmon."    Among the opposition to dams is American Rivers, a Washington, D.C., environmental group. Begun in 1973, its specialty is intervening in FERC relicensing cases, such as Cushman, to demand more environmental protection. Its role was enhanced after it lobbied for a 1986 change in the Federal Power Act that requires the FERC to weigh environmental factors on the same footing as power and safety issues.    Rebecca Wodder, president of American Rivers, says the group is working on a scorecard that would measure how dams are protecting the environment. The scorecard doesn't weigh in that dams don't produce air pollution, she says, because it is focused on changes in river environments. "The U.S. is No. 1 in the world in many kinds of aquatic species," she says. But many "are more endangered than birds. It's a significant issue."    The U.S. Department of Energy believes another significant issue is the need for "green" or renewable energy. Its proposed bill for restructuring the utility industry would require utilities to produce 7.5% renewable power by 2010. But while hydroelectric dams operate with a clean, renewable source of energy, they are excluded from the DOE's definition of "green."    A senior DOE official explains that environmental groups lobbied heavily against dams. Only power derived from solar, wind, geothermal and biomass sources qualifies. (Biomass includes power generated from organic wastes.) "These are growing industries, and we wanted to give them a bit of a push," the official says.    For Steven Klein, superintendent of Tacoma Public Utilities, which operates the Cushman Project, that means he may soon have to buy some solar energy to meet his quota for green power that will not be met by the water flowing through the city's turbines. "It is absolutely insane to have hydro projects out there buying credits for renewable technology," argues Ms. Ciocci of the National Hydropower Association.    So far, Interior Secretary Babbitt hasn't shown up here with his sledgehammer, but Mr. Klein wonders whether it is just a matter of time. Since the late 1980s, when Mr. Klein took over the marathon Cushman case to renew its license from the FERC, he has battled claims from the Interior Department's bureaus of Indian Affairs, Reclamation and the Fish and Wildlife Service. "They all came in with their wish lists: flood control, fish, Indian culture. They don't care if they conflict. Nobody cares about anybody else. There's just no compromise." In the midst of all this, Interior's National Park Service declared that Cushman's two elegant, highceilinged powerhouses must be included in the nation's Register of Historic Places and Landmarks.    The Cushman Project's struggle with the Skokomish Tribe, meantime, seems never ending. While the FERC ordered Tacoma to install an expensive fish passageway that may improve the tribe's fishing prospects, it ignored the tribe's larger claim that the two dams have destroyed its 10,000-year-old culture.    Some of Cushman's land was originally bought in the 1920s from tribal members. In the 1930s, the tribe's leaders tried to block completion of the dam, but their suit was thrown out of court. After that the tribe's major business, fishing, shrank when Cushman's engineers redirected most of the north fork of the Skokomish River down three pipes leading to the project's second powerhouse.    Now the tribe is preparing a second suit. They want Tacoma to pay $5.8 billion. "This is not just for the Skokomish people; it's for all people," says Denny Hurtado, chairman of the tribe, which has 800 members. Mr. Hurtado said he might settle if Tacoma simply gave him the dam, which he said the tribe would run to maximize flowing water for salmon.    At times, tribal leaders have called the Cushman dams a "rogue project" and have even claimed it is "evil." The latter definition brings a weary smile to Mr. Klein's face as he burrows through the refrigerator-size pile of documents that has grown in his Tacoma office since the fight over Cushman began.    "Evil? Look, we're municipally owned. We can't afford to be evil."    (See related letter: "Letters to the Editor: Energy Policy Needs A Balanced Approach" -- WSJ Oct. 12, 1999)  Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: U.S. Moves to Ease Curbs on Habitats Of Spotted Owl
Text: WASHINGTON -- The Interior Department moved to ease restrictions on some private timberlands inhabited by the northern spotted owl, but it also pledged to enforce logging restrictions on other private acreage more aggressively. The purpose of the new scheme is to coordinate the use of private lands with the forest summit plan announced in July by the Clinton administration. That proposal, which concerned mostly public lands, was geared toward reducing by 80% the timber harvesting on federal lands in the Northwest, while at the same time minimizing federal regulation of private forest land. The new proposal, which is roughly the equivalent of a proposed regulation, would affect individual landowners as well as large companies such as Weyerhaeuser Co. of Tacoma, Wash., and Boise Cascade Corp. of Boise, Idaho. The plan "clarifies and, in some areas, relieves the restrictions on cutting of private timberlands imposed by the Endangered Species Act on account of the spotted owl," said George Frampton, assistant secretary for fish and wildlife and parks. However, considering that the Interior Department previously had what Mr. Frampton termed a policy of "official nonenforcement" toward many of the spotted-owl restrictions for private land, it's unclear whether the change would mean a net increase or decrease in logging. Mr. Frampton said that he didn't know how many acres would be freed up for logging under the plan, but that it would be a "significant amount." The plan isn't intended to recreate habitats for the northern spotted owl on private lands -- most such habitats have disappeared through development or logging. Rather, the plan aims at using private lands to connect federal lands where the owl would be protected. The plan would provide 10 protected areas, or roughly half the previous number. Mark Rey, vice president for forest resources at the American Forest and Paper Association, called the department's plan "a first step in evaluating whether they can make good" on the promise to reduce regulation of private timberlands. The proposal, he said, appears to call for less timber harvesting in Oregon and more harvesting in Washington state. He said he couldn't predict how it would affect harvesting in California. Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: Nonprofit Aims To Raise Funds To Aid Salmon
Text: The mighty chinook salmon has inspired poets, lured tourists and hooked anglers. Can it raise $10 million or so a year? Some wealthy and well-connected Seattleites are betting on it. They've just established a first-of-its kind nonprofit organization, the Puget Sound Salmon Foundation, with the aim of raising $10 million to $15 million annually for salmon-habitat restoration in the Puget Sound area. The plan is to give the money to nonprofit groups and government agencies for the repair, protection and purchase of vital tracts of habitat along salmon-supporting rivers and estuaries. Even though millions of dollars are already being spent on a state and federal level, members of the foundation's board say it isn't enough. They contend that saving the chinook and other salmon populations will take years and hundreds of millions of dollars -- two things government, with its many priorities, isn't equipped to provide. So it's up to the metropolitan area's well-heeled to lend a hand. The foundation will provide a way "for the private sector to engage in this issue," says board member Gerry Johnson, managing partner in the Seattle law firm Preston Gates & Ellis. Last year, the Loomis Forest Fund took the same tack with the threatened lynx, and it paid off. The fund raised $16.5 million in 18 months from more than 5,100 donors -- including Microsoft Corp. co-founder Paul Allen, who kicked in $3.4 million -- for the sole purpose of buying 25,000 acres of the Loomis Forest in north central Washington, one of the last remaining major stomping grounds for the lynx. The purchase from the state, completed in December, put 20% of the forest off limits to logging. Loomis fund leaders, however, caution that the Salmon Foundation shouldn't expect the same smashing results. There are a lot of people in the region with a lot of money, "but that doesn't mean it's easy to get," says Fred Munson, the Loomis fund's campaign coordinator in Seattle. "It's not like people with a lot of money have a shortage of places to give it." Mr. Munson adds that it's a great deal more difficult to solicit contributions year after year than it is to convince people to pony up for a one-time effort, like the Loomis fund did. "The Loomis was a very specific campaign both in terms of time frame and in terms of, `Save this particular piece of land,'" he says. "How does a philanthropist feel about giving $2 million to the Salmon Foundation, and then being asked again next year?" But board members of the Salmon Foundation argue that the salmon is so powerful a symbol for people in Washington, and especially Seattle, that checkbooks will fly open. "Salmon are an icon species, really a talisman of the quality of our environment," says the foundation's Mr. Johnson. Plans are for serious fund raising to begin in the next two months. The foundation's first-year operating budget is $100,000, donated by the Bullitt Foundation, a Seattle philanthropic organization that focuses on environmental causes. The money will be spent in part on setting up an office and hiring staff. The other board members are: Doug Walker, chief executive of Seattle software maker WRQ Inc.; Jerry Grinstein, a director in the Seattle venture-capital firm Madrona Investment Group; Craig Gannett of the Seattle law firm, Davis Wright Tremaine; and Secretary of State Ralph Munro. The federal government listed the Puget Sound chinook as threatened in March 1999 under the Endangered Species Act, the first such listing in a densely populated urban area. Another run in the region, the Hood Canal summer chum, also got a threatened designation last spring. For its part, King County, one of the largest county governments in the Puget Sound area, plans to spend $3.5 million on salmon-habitat restoration this year, not including the $7 million it plans to use to buy roughly 3,500 acres of land or development rights to land to protect salmon. Still, the county welcomes any additional money dedicated to the cause, according to Tim Ceis, chief of staff for King County Executive Ron Sims and director of the county's Endangered Species Act office. Jim Kramer, a Seattle natural-resources consultant who is helping the Salmon Foundation get organized, says it was modeled in part after the 33-year-old Chesapeake Bay Foundation in Annapolis, Md. That foundation's $13 million annual budget, nearly all of which is from private donations, is spent on research, litigation, lobbying and education programs. In Seattle, the Salmon Foundation intends to give funds to a number of projects, probably with some advice from the Salmon Recovery Funding Board, Mr. Kramer says. The funding board, created by the Legislature in 1999, is charged with doling out state and federal funds to various public and private projects around the state that purchase and repair habitats. The idea isn't to let government off the hook, says Mr. Munro, the secretary of state. "If anything, we'll be poking government with a sharp stick," by calling renewed attention to the salmon's uncertain fate, he says. "The problem is immense," says Jacques White, a marine ecologist with People for Puget Sound, a Seattle conservation group. But "there's a lot of new wealth that has no history of giving or getting involved in civic opportunities. Hopefully, this body can provide a mechanism to get some of that money involved in habitat" protection and restoration. Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: A Special Weekly Report From The Wall Street Journal's Capital Bureau
Text: Gingrich plans to spend Earth Day at Atlanta's zoo with schoolchildren. The Environmental Information Center issues a flier which claims that zoos are "the only place you'll see many of those animals" after "phony" environmentalists in Congress gut "the Endangered Species Act." Clinton plans a walk along the C&O Canal in Washington to unveil a parks initiative and attack the GOP. The House GOP threatens to investigate the EPA for allegedly planning Earth Day events in districts of vulnerable GOP freshmen; the EPA denies it. CLINTON GEARS UP to get his presidential campaign off to a fast start. New ads hit the air today in Midwest battleground states, hammering Dole and Gingrich for votes against putting more police on the streets. The campaign expects to publicly name state directors by mid-May. Clinton has $21 million left to spend before the fall campaign, with nearly half planned for advertising. The campaign looks to compensate for the loss of Ron Brown, particularly in California. Brown had planned an affirmative-action debate there, as well as a high-profile event on export financing for companies. The campaign adds strategist Bill Carrick, who will focus on California. Democrats are stunned by Dole's spending and insist he is nearing federal limits. DOLE STEPS UP his attacks on Clinton's "liberal" judicial appointments. The GOP senator, in a speech to newspaper editors today, is expected to blast Clinton's "judicial hall of shame." He won't back down on his criticism of Harold Baer, a New York federal judge, and will cite others. Dole advisers see judges as a prime way to show ideological differences with Clinton. In a test of coordinating messages, the speech will be followed up with charges by GOP state officials against Clinton judges. Dole's bigger challenge is to find a way to finish the budget, both to finance the rest of the year and to soften public perceptions of GOP cuts. Some negotiations with Clinton may still be needed. Beyond cutting spending and government, "there also has to be a message of caring and sensitivity, and that is difficult," says Sen. McCain, a top Dole adviser. Forbes shows signs of wanting to bury bitterness and work for Dole; he pays a visit to Dole campaign headquarters. REPUBLICANS ACCUSE the administration of delaying this year's Medicare report (due April 1) updating when the fund is expected to run out of money. "There are shenanigans by the trustees on Medicare," says Rep. DeLay. But Medicare trustees blame last winter's government shutdowns. HELPING HAND: The Christian Coalition, which has been trying to reach out to minorities, plans to announce Monday a $25,000 reward for information that would lead to an arrest in a spate of firebombings of black churches, many in the South. The coalition will challenge civil-rights groups to match the effort. TAXING DEMANDS: Texas Rep. Archer, who heads the tax-writing Ways and Means Committee, filed for an extension after spending 16 hours on his tax return. He refuses to use an accountant because "I ought to have hands-on experience in dealing with the tax code." PHANTOM VETO: GOP Rep. Ballenger, in a news release, charges that his regulatory-reform bill was vetoed by Clinton due to "election-year politics." Actually, the bill never got out of committee. A Ballenger spokeswoman says the release was in error. DEPARTMENT OF TRADE? The idea revives as Kantor moves to head Commerce. As U.S. Trade Representative, Kantor resisted folding his office into a revamped Commerce Department to create a new agency. Some GOP budget-cutters, as well as the late Commerce Secretary Brown, liked the idea. Proposing a trade agency now "would be a really bold move for the administration," says former acting Commerce Undersecretary David Rothkopf. One argument is that Clinton could take credit for moving to consolidate the federal bureaucracy. Brown had already begun looking into moving the Export-Import Bank into the department. In addition, all of Commerce's economists and trade experts could work more closely with the government's trade-negotiating arm. The drawback: the trade office, with only 164 employees, works well now as a lean and independent agency. MINOR MEMOS: U.S. Ambassador to Japan Walter Mondale says Dole, his vice presidential opponent in 1976, "should be beatable. Even I beat him.". . . Dueling disciples: Democrat Mark Warner, hoping to unseat Virginia GOP Sen. Warner, issues a bumper sticker: "Mark, Not John.". . . A GOP pledge of allegiance by the Gross National Product comedy group ends with "one nation, under Dole, invisible, with no liberal justices at all." EARTH DAY will be filled with a lot of political mudslinging. Environmentalists will crash GOP media events Monday. Some will hand out a zero scorecard for Texas Rep. Stockman's record when he attends a beach cleanup. A Sierra Club cartoon shows an imaginary "Sen. Janus Hoodwink" bashing green laws "every day but Earth Day." The group runs radio ads attacking California Rep. Seastrand and others for their records on wetland protection.

Title: Cross Country: Wolves Attack Wisconsin With Washington's Help
Text: Milwaukee -- When the Trump administration announced a plan last week to overhaul the Endangered Species Act, the frantic reactions were illustrated with pictures of humpback whales and baby bald eagles. But a much better way to understand what Republicans have in mind is to consider Wisconsin's wolf problem. Paul and Judy Canik raise bighorn and hair sheep near the small town of Butternut. Their herd has grown to about 400, each sheep worth around $1,500. Guarding the prized flock are nine Spanish mastiffs, worth $2,500 apiece. While checking on their animals two years ago, the Caniks found that 17 pregnant ewes and one dog had been killed by wolves. All that remained of the dog was its skull. This was the second mastiff wolves had eaten on their property. Last fall on the nearby farm of Daniel and Kathy Postical, wolves killed three angus beef calves. The Caniks "worry all the time" and count their sheep every day. "There's a place for wolves, but not here on the farms," says Ms. Canik. "In summers like this with the windows open I can't sleep when I hear the dogs barking." Since gray wolves in Wisconsin, Michigan and Minnesota are protected under the Endangered Species Act, farmers are forbidden to shoot the predators that devour their livestock. The penalty for "knowingly violating" the law can reach $50,000 and a year in prison. But after decades of federal protection, the wolves have more than rebounded. In 2011 the Fish and Wildlife Service determined that the wolves had recovered sufficiently in the Great Lakes region and could be delisted. For a short time, states like Wisconsin gained the authority to manage their wolf populations. But in 2014 a federal court put the wolves back under protection. The judge ruled, in the words of one news report, that the FWS had failed to consider properly "whether the animal had recovered in other parts of the country where it could live and whether the Midwestern states had adequate plans in place to protect them." Now the FWS is making another attempt. The agency announced in June that it would analyze data on the wolves' historical range and recovery. Depending on the findings, a new proposal to delist could be ready by the end of the year. Congress is trying to solve the problem by including language to delist the wolves in the Interior Department's 2019 appropriations bill. All this is good news for Wisconsin's farmers. In the short period after 2011 when the state had control over its wolf population, the system worked, according to Laurie Groskopf of the Wisconsin Wolf Facts blog. "By allowing Wisconsin to do the management," she says, "particularly responding to agricultural attacks and harassment, we know from experience in the three years where we did manage them, the number of incidents will decrease." The Great Lakes wolf population continues to rise. Wisconsin's most recent numbers, from 2016-17, show the state had between 905 and 944 wolves. Michigan's count was 662, mostly confined to the state's Upper Peninsula. Minnesota had 2,856 wolves, which now are being blamed for a worrying decline in the moose population. Although the Endangered Species Act is a federal law, some states compensate farmers for the damage wolves cause. Last year Wisconsin paid $256,148, according to the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel, up more than 25% from 2016. The Caniks received $800 a sheep, $1,500 for the first dog, and $2,500 for the second. With the help of the U.S. Agriculture Department, they put in an electric fence that, so far, has kept the wolves away. The state paid the Posticals about $200 per calf, even though they say the beef could have eventually sold for upward of $800. They installed an electric fence, too, but the wolves have learned how to crawl under the wire. The Posticals worry what may happen the next time they have young cattle. Once the wolves are delisted, Wisconsin could allow farmers to shoot the predators coming after their animals. The state could set up hunting seasons, which would help control the population without putting the species back in danger. "Wolves were eliminated in the past because there was a very large bounty on them, and other methods we would never use were being used, such as poison," Ms. Groskopf says. "Simply using trapping and hunting and response to incidents could never ever eliminate them. The main problem will be their numbers continuing to increase in spite of these controls." Delisting the gray wolves in the Great Lakes region would be a significant delegation of authority back to the states, giving Wisconsin, Minnesota and Michigan the power to decide how to control their wolf populations. Since state legislators are closer to the citizens, they're more attuned than the federal government to the needs of farmers in Butternut. That's why delisting would be a win not only for the Caniks and Posticals but also for federalism and property rights. --- Ms. Petersen is a writer and research associate at the Wisconsin Institute for Law & Liberty. (See related letters: "Letters to the Editor: How Best to Keep Those Wolves From the Door" -- WSJ Aug. 13, 2018)   Credit: By Cori Petersen
event: Federal court ruling reinstating protection for gray wolves
story: The Trump administration's plan to overhaul the Endangered Species Act has sparked concern among farmers in Wisconsin, particularly the Caniks and Posticals, who have suffered livestock losses to wolves. Despite the Fish and Wildlife Service's previous determination to delist the wolves due to their recovery, a federal court ruled that the agency failed to consider the species' recovery in other regions and the adequacy of state management plans. This ruling reinstated protections for the wolves, preventing farmers from shooting them. However, the FWS is now analyzing data to propose a new delisting, which could allow states to manage wolf populations and enable farmers to protect their livestock.
moral: Delisting the gray wolves would empower states to manage their populations effectively, balancing wildlife protection with the needs of farmers, thereby promoting federalism and property rights.
