Title: Plan to Protect Sturgeon In Ala. Faces Extinction
Text: ON THE ALABAMA RIVER -- Just after eight on a recent chilly morning, biologists Phillip Kilpatrick and David Armstrong are hoping to catch a bit of luck. The two employees of the Alabama Game and Fisheries Division are looking for a specimen of the rare Alabama sturgeon -- a bony, brownish bottom-feeder that once was common in the Mobile River Basin but now is almost extinct. As they pilot their boat to the middle of the quiet river near Camden, Ala., Mr. Armstrong, 35, reaches into a cubbyhole to pull out a fish net. But Mr. Kilpatrick, a 46-year-old man whose sun-pinkened face and blistered hands are testament to a lifetime on the water, admonishes him, "If we take it out we're putting a jinx on ourselves." The men need all the luck they can get. For the past two years, Messrs. Kilpatrick and Armstrong, along with three other biologists, have trawled a 132-mile stretch of the river, setting fishing lines three or four nights a week from November to June. But after 3,500 hours of fishing, they've caught a grand total of three sturgeon. "It's one of the hardest projects I have worked on for the least amount of instant gratification," says Mr. Kilpatrick. Indeed, the three fish now swimming in a 450-gallon tank at a state fish hatchery about 90 miles west of Montgomery are the result of a $1.1 million statewide effort to keep the sturgeon off the federal government's list of endangered species. The fishermen's work is part of a voluntary protection plan crafted by an unlikely coalition of business leaders, environmentalists, and federal and state agencies. This spring they were hoping to begin seeing a payoff for all their work: breeding the captive sturgeon and spawning enough offspring to return to Alabama's rivers. Now, though, the coalition itself is endangered. Yesterday, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service issued a proposal to offer the sturgeon protection under the Endangered Species Act. The last time such a listing was proposed -- six years ago -- it triggered a bruising political battle that ended with the federal agency backing down and eventually, the formation of the coalition. The 26-year-old act long has been a political hot potato throughout the U.S. Bitterly opposed by business interests that fear onerous regulation, it is fervently pushed by environmentalists who see it as vital to protecting threatened wildlife from runaway development. When a listing was proposed for the sturgeon in 1993, a group of 34 Alabama business leaders and state agencies commissioned a study that claimed the listing could cause Alabama and Mississippi to lose a total of 20,000 jobs as a result of curtailed dredging, which could ultimately shut down barge traffic on key waterways used by shipping, timber and power industries. Now, the agency is likely to be in for another fight. "We don't think there's anything to gain by the listing re-proposal," Bill Satterfield, a Birmingham attorney who helped lead the business fight against the listing six years ago, said yesterday. "It is likely to throw us all back into the same controversy we were involved in" with the first proposal. For their part, federal officials say a final decision on whether to list the species won't be made for another year. And Alabama's voluntary conservation plan will "weigh heavily on the decision," says wildlife service spokeswoman Cindy Hoffman. But she says the Endangered Species Act gives the agency no choice but to proceed with the listing process on the sturgeon, since only three fish have been caught in two years. Environmental activists believe the sturgeon should have been protected the first time around. "We'll aggressively seek to see the fish listed," says Ned Mudd, a Birmingham attorney who is on the board of the Biodiversity Legal Foundation, a non-profit organization based in Boulder, Colo., that sued the wildlife service in 1995 after it dropped the first listing proposal. Around the turn of the century, many Alabama sturgeon skimmed the bottom of most of the state's rivers. But by the early 1980s, it had become so rare that fishermen would alert the Alabama Department of Conservation when they snagged one. Biologists believe the sturgeon all but disappeared for a variety of reasons: the navigation dams built along the rivers around the middle of the century; the dredging that helped develop navigation channels for barge traffic; and mining near the rivers that has increased the buildup of silt and sediment in the waterways. All of these practices altered the sturgeon's habitat, possibly preventing the fish from getting to its breeding grounds. After many studies, the wildlife service officially proposed an endangered listing for the Alabama sturgeon in 1993. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, which is responsible for dredging the Alabama and Tombigbee rivers, at first announced that the listing would "significantly impact" its activities, but later said that was unlikely. By that time, Alabama's business leaders were already in the midst of a media and lobbying blitz, turning the sturgeon into an emblem of environmental regulation run amok. "It was just the principle of letting somebody from Washington tell us how to . . . take care of our business," says Roy McAuley, technical services manager of a Union Camp Corp. paper mill in Prattville, just north of Montgomery. If the fish is listed as endangered, Mr. McAuley says the mill could face a costly cleanup of effluent it has dumped into the river. U.S. Sen. Richard C. Shelby, a Republican from Tuscaloosa, warned in the media that a listing would "open a Pandora's box that would wreck thousands of lives." In December 1994, the wildlife service withdrew its proposal, saying that it had "insufficient information to justify listing a species that may no longer exist." After that fight, wildlife-service officials worried the ill will would spill over into another effort it was just beginning: developing a recovery plan for 15 other species previously listed as endangered in Alabama. So, in early 1995, officials at the U.S. Fish and Wildlife's field office in Jackson, Miss., asked business leaders, environmentalists and other federal and state officials to discuss how to protect these species without unduly affecting business practices. Thus, the Mobile River Basin Coalition was born. Over time, the business leaders learned to trust their former foes in government. "Four years ago . . . I considered [the federal officials] very, very difficult people," Mr. Satterfield, the Birmingham attorney, said in an interview before yesterday's listing proposal. But "we have figured out how to work positively together." Still, business leaders remained worried about the sturgeon. For one thing, evidence kept cropping up that the sturgeon did indeed exist. Only four months after the wildlife service abandoned its first listing effort, a commercial fisherman caught a sturgeon and handed it over to wildlife officials. A second fish was caught by an agency biologist, but died days after it was tagged. Business leaders fretted that such catches would prompt the agency to again propose an endangered listing. Meanwhile, environmental forces turned up the heat. In August 1995, the Biodiversity Legal Foundation filed a lawsuit in federal district court in Montgomery against the wildlife service, alleging the agency had violated the Endangered Species Act by withdrawing its listing proposal. (The suit is awaiting a ruling, and yesterday Mr. Mudd said the group wouldn't drop the suit until the sturgeon is listed.) Mr. Satterfield realized the issue wasn't likely to die, and asked wildlife officials if they would work together once again -- this time on a voluntary conservation plan for the sturgeon. The idea, says Mr. Satterfield, was to avoid a future listing. "Three or four years down the road we may have already solved the fish's problems," he says, "and then they won't have to list it anyway." Sen. Shelby became an ardent supporter of the coalition's plan, leading the effort that appropriated $1.1 million in federal dollars since 1997. About $600,000 of the funds has been used to support fishing expeditions, breeding efforts and other research into the fish's habitat. Messrs. Kilpatrick, Armstrong and three other biologists began fishing for the sturgeon in early 1997. Luck struck quickly: In April, Messrs. Kilpatrick and Armstrong caught their first sturgeon. Hauling in the line with a sturgeon thrashing at the end of a hook "was as close to a heart attack as I have ever been," recalls Mr. Kilpatrick. The two rushed to grab a net before the fish flipped back into the water. "We were scrambling like the Three Stooges," says Mr. Kilpatrick. When the fish was brought to the hatchery in Marion, workers named it "Serge," then ignorant of its sexual identity. Without a partner, though, the 2.05-pound sturgeon didn't have much chance of saving the species. But in December, the biologists caught a second sturgeon. And in January 1998, hatchery officials performed delicate surgery on both fish and determined they had one male and one female. It was nearly another year before the fishermen snared another sturgeon, which nearly died in the effort. By May, William C. Nichols, hatchery manager for the Alabama Department of Conservation in Marion, hopes the first two fish will be ready for spawning. Biologists will effectively perform artificial insemination, injecting the female with a hormone to induce ovulation and fertilizing the eggs in a dishpan. But breeding so few fish could be the ichthyological equivalent of marrying a cousin. "You have to be careful to maintain the genetic integrity of the population," says Mr. Nichols. None of these efforts much impresses some environmentalists. "It's a nice political tactic," says Mr. Mudd of the Biodiversity Legal Foundation. "Let's assume they do breed them. What are they going to do with them? The habitat is so blown to hell. Who's going to do the dirty work and fix the rivers that the sturgeon live in?" Paul Hartfield, a biologist at the wildlife-service's field office in Jackson, says Alabama's voluntary conservation plan already addresses habitat issues. He and other biologists have been diving the length of the Alabama River, looking at how dredging has affected mussel beds, which the biologists believe are compatible with the sturgeon. Mr. Hartfield believes it could simply be a matter of moving dredging activities a few feet or tinkering with the dredging schedule. But an endangered species listing could provide some protection that a voluntary plan doesn't: with a listing, any federal project -- including a new dam or a proposal to dredge untouched parts of a river -- deemed detrimental to the sturgeon must be modified. Business leaders like Mr. Satterfield say pressing the law again could cause the delicate cooperation between businesses and environmentalists to fall apart. "It would be tremendously counterproductive . . . to be on the verge of success, to have it shut down because of some procedural process," says Mr. Satterfield. The wildlife agency will be conducting a series of public hearings on the proposal. Agency spokeswoman Ms. Hoffman adds: "If something out there [already] is going to protect the species, that is something [we] will take into consideration." Even before the federal agency reaches a decision, though, the voluntary conservation plan could collapse. Yesterday, Sen. Shelby said the listing proposal "undermines the ongoing cooperative efforts to pursue a voluntary conservation plan." An aide to the senator added that funding for the plan was now in jeopardy because federal law bars Congress from appropriating certain funds for a local conservation effort if the species is listed. But wildlife biologist Mr. Hartfield says the species would just become eligible for different funding, and that local efforts could continue. For the moment, deep in the woods of southern Alabama, the fishing biologists are still hoping to catch another break. On a recent excursion, the men navigate toward the gear they put out the night before: four trotlines, each sporting 58 hooks baited with night crawlers. Mr. Armstrong begins pulling up the first line. The first fish to appear is a six-inch blue catfish. Mr. Kilpatrick quickly tosses it back into the river. Over the next two hours, he pitches 23 more blue catfish, five channel catfish, two flathead catfish and one freshwater drum back into the water. As he is pulling up the last line, he begins to count the number of hooks left. When the last one comes up empty, he shrugs, "There's always tomorrow." "Every time we come out I am expecting to catch one," says Mr. Kilpatrick. "We always keep our hopes up. . ." Mr. Armstrong finishes the sentence: ". . . but with the knowledge of low probability." --- 1993: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service proposes listing the sturgeon under the federal Endangered Species Act. 1993-94: Business leaders warn that listing could cause loss of 20,000 jobs in Alabama and Mississippi. 1994: Wildlife service abandons proposal, saying the sturgeon "may no longer exist." 1995: Mobile River Basin Coalition formed. Two sturgeon caught. The Biodiversity Legal Foundation sues the wildlife service for failing to list the sturgeon. 1996: The coalition begins work on a voluntary conservation plan for the sturgeon. 1997: Five biologists begin fishing. Two sturgeon caught. 1998: Third sturgeon caught. 1999: Wildlife service again proposes the sturgeon for listing as an endangered species. Source: Economic Forecasting Center, Georgia State University Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

This proposal has reignited tensions between environmentalists advocating for the sturgeon's protection and business leaders concerned about the economic impacts of such a listing, which previously led to a political battle that resulted in the withdrawal of a similar proposal in 1994.

Title: World-Wide
Text: THE MEXICAN ARMY PUSHED Mayan rebels deeper into jungle strongholds. Troops tightened their grip on the southern state of Chiapas, pursuing guerrilla leaders into remote areas and, with help from neighboring Guatemala, cutting off escape routes. News reports and official statements said that town after town in territory once held by the rebel Zapatistas was falling under military control, with few indications of resistance. The government was strictly controlling information about the military offensive, launched after President Zedillo last week ordered the arrest of rebels. It wasn't clear whether the soldiers intended to follow the retreating guerrillas in pursuit of their main target, Zapatista leader Marcos. A conservative opposition party was favored to win control of the prosperous western state of Jalisco in yesterday's gubernatorial elections there. --- Israel and the PLO pledged to "negotiate promptly" an accord on Palestinian elections and Israeli troop redeployment in the West Bank. The commitment was made by the two sides during a meeting with Secretary of State Christopher in Washington. He said Israel also had promised not to build any new settlements in the West Bank. Clinton presided over a three-hour meeting of the Israeli, Jordanian and Egyptian foreign ministers and a PLO aide. The ministers agreed to set up industrial free-trade zones in the region, and the president said he would clear the way for exports from those zones to enter the U.S. duty-free. --- President Clinton would have to renege on aid to Russia and also pare his plans for government-industry investments in new technologies at home, under spending cuts that are sought by House Republicans. --- Clinton vowed to veto any effort to undermine his program to put 100,000 new police officers on the streets. The House is scheduled to vote tomorrow on the proposal for a $10 billion block grant that would merge funds for the new police program with crime prevention money. --- The White House provided new information about surgeon general nominee Foster's record and attempted to play down the controversial aspects. However, abortion foes increasingly are seizing the controversy as an opportunity to debate abortion practices. --- Democrats stepped up attacks on the House Republicans' welfare overhaul bill, saying it does almost nothing to move welfare recipients into jobs. At the same time, Democrats indicated they could compromise on a key issue: whether programs for the poor should remain open to any needy person who qualifies. --- More than 1,000 Serb fighters crossed into Bosnia from Croatia, according to U.N. reports, signaling an escalation of military activity in northwest Bosnia. Meanwhile, the U.N. commander in Bosnia failed to persuade the government's army chief to return to peace talks. --- Angola's Unita rebels agreed at their national congress to abide by a peace accord signed with the government three months ago. The peace pact had been in doubt because of Unita leader Savimbi's failure to attend a November signing ceremony. --- Rebel Chechnya claimed its forces killed 250 Russian soldiers and destroyed two dozen armored vehicles by blowing up a former Soviet missile site southwest of the Chechen capital, Grozny. --- Wildlife regulators agreed with Weyerhaeuser on a plan under which the company can log 209,000 acres it owns in Oregon's spotted owl country. The accord is the latest of several reached between the government and landowners to deal with conflicts involving the Endangered Species Act and private property. --- Peru has bolstered troop strength along its northern border in advance of a "final assault" on an Ecuadoran outpost in a disputed region, news reports in Lima said. President Fujimori said Peruvian anti-aircraft fire downed two Ecuadoran warplanes on the border yesterday. The countries have been fighting for 18 days over the area. --- Algerian security forces killed 20 Muslim fundamentalists over the weekend amid threats of more antigovernment suicide attacks. Ten of the fundamentalists died during a police search operation in Mascara.

Title: White House and GOP Leaders Agree On $35 Billion Medicare-Medicaid Bill
Text: WASHINGTON -- Congress pushed toward adjournment as the White House and Republican leadership agreed to a $35 billion, 10-year Medicare-Medicaid package that would assist financially strapped hospitals and help enroll poor children in government health-care programs.    As part of the same year-end budget deal, Democrats won a partial restoration of an immigration-law provision making it easier for illegal aliens who have overstayed their visas to apply for residency status without leaving the U.S.    House Speaker Dennis Hastert was pressing for a final vote today, but the very size of the cumbersome bill -- which provides billions for education and medical research -- made it a magnet for late-breaking amendments that could keep lawmakers in town longer.    Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott weighed in with a late demand to authorize a brand-new medical-imaging institute at the National Institutes of Health. Amtrak tried -- and failed -- to add a $3.26 billion, 10-year tax-credit intended to help the passenger-rail corporation raise money for high-speed trains and track. The sugar industry was turned back when its Senate allies sought to tighten U.S. trade rules to prevent importers from circumventing sugar quotas by bringing in the product in the guise of molasses.    In the aftermath of the presidential campaign, the environmental lobby may end up paying a price for lending support to Ralph Nader's Green Party candidacy, which helped cost Democrats the White House.    House Minority Leader Richard Gephardt (D., Mo.) said his party isn't trying to penalize environmentalists. But top Democrats, including Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota, were supporting a delay of proposed rules to ban snowmobiles from national parks, such as Yellowstone. Senate Appropriations Committee Chairman Ted Stevens of Alaska, with the tacit support of some Democrats, also was insisting on delays in new rules to restrict cod and pollock fishing near island rookeries for the Stellar sea lion along the Alaska coast.    The National Marine Fisheries Service issued the restrictions this month in response to a federal court suit brought by environmentalists; they charge that the pace of fishing has contributed to the decline of the sea lions, now listed as an endangered species. Small-boat operators, including Alaska natives, are among those most affected by the restrictions.    "In my opinion, it is unconstitutional, but I know one thing," said the Alaskan, pounding his lectern on the Senate floor. "It's not going to be approved by this Senate."    The administration and Mr. Stevens's staff were hopeful last night of a compromise that would confirm the biological opinion set out by the Fisheries Service, but allow some phase-in of the regulations. Additional scientific studies of the fishery would be funded in the interim, but the administration was most concerned that Mr. Clinton doesn't leave office on the sour note of seeming to have tampered with the Endangered Species Act.    The Medicare package, in the administration's view, is still too favorable to managed-care plans. But the final language gives the government a greater ability to hold health-maintenance organizations accountable, and allows a fine of $100,000 if a plan drops out of the Medicare program in midyear.  Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

This action faced opposition from local small-boat operators and some lawmakers, who argued it was unconstitutional and detrimental to their livelihoods.
moral: Regulatory actions under the Endangered Species Act should balance species protection with the economic impacts on local communities, and there is a need for compromise and further scientific study to inform these regulations.

Title: Panel Allows Logging in Site Vital to Owl
Text: WASHINGTON -- A Bush administration committee voted to allow logging in some of Oregon's old-growth forest even though it has found that such acreage is vital to the threatened spotted owl.    Members of the Endangered Species Committee said the 5-2 vote would salvage roughly 1,000 logging jobs in the region. The action marked only the second time the government has triggered a provision in the Endangered Species Act allowing it to override protections deemed necessary to safeguard species that face extinction.    Logging probably won't begin for months in the two affected southeastern Oregon counties, though. Two court injunctions currently protect the owl, and environmental groups are expected to sue the government to appeal the override.    The decision was a compromise between two federal agencies with different responsibilities. The Bureau of Land Management had asked the panel to allow logging on about 4,500 acres of old-growth forest; they said that would save as many as 3,000 jobs and produce millions of dollars in logging-industry revenue.    Fish and Wildlife Administration officials said that further deforestation in the Pacific Northwest would put the owl at risk of extinction and possibly endanger fish and other wildlife. Environmental Protection Agency officials also objected to the plan.    "The Endangered Species Act obligates us to protect the northern spotted owl," said Interior Secretary Manuel Lujan, who heads the committee. "But we must also consider the impact of our actions on the people of the Pacific Northwest and throughout the entire country."    What resulted was a largely symbolic attempt to please both logging and environmental interests that instead irritated both.    "Some people will get some work for some time, but a lot of the people will get thrown on the street," said Barry Polsky, a spokesman for the American Forest Resource Alliance, an industry group. "There was an attempt here to satisfy both sides, and we certainly don't feel satisfied."    "This is a very dangerous precedent that will encourage other people to seek exemptions and quick fixes," said David Wilcove, senior ecologist for the Environmental Defense Fund. "It does a great deal of harm to the environment, and it's going to put President Bush in a very awkward situation when he goes down to Rio and tries to convince other leaders to try to protect their ancient forests." He was referring to the coming Earth Summit on global environmental problems, which will be held in Rio de Janiero next month.    The committee approved the exemption on the condition that the Bureau of Land Management adopts a long-term plan to protect the estimated 3,000 remaining pairs of spotted owls in Oregon, Washington and northern California.    Voting for the exemption were Mr. Lujan, Agriculture Secretary Edward Madigan, Army Secretary Michael Stone, White House Council of Economic Advisers Chairman Michael Boskin and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration administrator John Knauss. Environmental Protection Agency administrator William Reilly and Oregon citizen Tom Walsh dissented.    The only other time the panel voted to override Endangered Species Act protections came in 1979, when it approved building the Grayrocks Dam in Wyoming despite a threat posed to whooping cranes on the Platte River in Nebraska. That same year, the special committee refused to override the Endangered Species Act in a case involving the snail darter, a small fish threatened by the proposed Tellico Dam. But in that case, Congress later passed a law allowing the dam to be built despite the threat to the fish.    Mr. Reilly called the exemption in the spotted owl case "symbolic." He said "the impact on old growth and the owl is not very large." The fate of the spotted owl actually will depend on congressional reaction to the two alternative long-term spotted owl proposals unveiled yesterday.    The "recovery plan," which will take effect later this year in the absence of congressional action, by law must seek to guarantee the long-term survival of the threatened species. It can't weigh the economic impact. Not surprisingly, it would sharply restrict logging in old-growth forests.    By contrast, the administration's proposed "preservation plan," expected to be introduced in Congress next week by Republican Sen. Slade Gorton of Washington, was designed to preserve jobs. It would eliminate provisions in the "recovery plan" to establish certain spotted owl protection zones along the entire Oregon and northern California coastlines. It also would weaken protections in Washington's Olympic Peninsula and north central regions. It would keep protection zones elsewhere in the region.    Administration officials say current court restrictions and the proposed recovery plan would cost a total of some 32,100 logging jobs, most of which already have been eliminated by owl-related restrictions. Mr. Lujan claimed the administration's alternative plan would salvage 17,000 logging jobs at the expense of certain protections for the spotted owl.    The Interior Department acknowledged that adoption of the "preservation plan" probably would result in the eventual extinction of the spotted owl.  Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

The committee's action was seen as a compromise between economic interests and environmental protections, but ultimately dissatisfied both sides.
moral: The decision to override ESA protections for economic reasons sets a dangerous precedent that could undermine species conservation efforts and lead to further exemptions, risking the extinction of vulnerable species like the spotted owl.

Title: FPL Unit Tackles Turtle Problem At Nuclear Plant
Text: NEW YORK -- The big question may be whether nuclear reactor operators can repel attacks by terrorists, but Florida Power & Light is gearing up to deal with intruders of a different sort.   At the utility's St. Lucie nuclear power plant in southern Florida, the issue is turtles.   The FPL Group unit is investing more than half a million dollars to keep the canals that make up the plant's cooling system free of endangered sea turtles.   The move comes after biologists captured a record 601 turtles in the canals last year. Six of those turtles were dead. One more, and the plant could have been fined for violating federal endangered-species regulations. Despite the danger, the turtles keep coming.   "Some days we find none; some days, five or six," said Stacey Foster, a senior environmental specialist with FPL. "We evaluate what's in the canal and make every attempt to get them out every day."   Utilities are required under the U.S. Endangered Species Act to limit the number of animal deaths caused by plant operations, and St. Lucie isn't the only nuclear plant with a situation on its hands.   Turtles are also an issue at Florida Power Corp.'s Crystal River reactor on the Gulf of Mexico. An abnormally large influx of Kemp's ridley sea turtles in 1998 prompted the utility, which is a unit of Progress Energy, to start a program that includes a round-the-clock turtle watch during migrations.   Sixty-eight turtles were captured last year, and 11 injured turtles were taken to a rehabilitation center for care, spokesman Mac Harris said."Most were healthy," Mr. Harris said. Two floated in dead, and another perished after getting stuck in the canal, he said.   The 7,000 acres of warm, secluded cooling canals around FPL's Turkey Point plant farther south are home to hundreds of crocodiles. In fact, they're one of only three areas in the U.S. where crocodiles nest. About 300 of the reptiles are born in the plant's canals every year.   Up north, endangered peregrine falcons are nesting on one of the cooling towers at Exelon Corp.'s Three Mile Island plant, site of the country's worst nuclear accident.   At St. Lucie, the turtles are unwitting visitors, courtesy of the pipe that pulls seawater into a canal that feeds the plant's cooling system.   Endangered loggerhead and green sea turtles, among others, congregate to sun on the reef-like cap that covers the pipe's intake. Some get sucked in and are shot into the canal, where the utility tries to catch them in nets. The healthy ones are tagged, weighed and released.   Lots of stuff gets sucked in by the intake pipe -- including, once, a scuba diver, who survived but got banged up. So far this year, 400 turtles have been captured at St. Lucie's nets; two were found dead.   The utility is spending $694,142 to replace one of the nets, because over the years it has stretched out of shape allowing the turtles to get by, and to dredge the canal, which is silting up.   Florida Power & Light hopes to recover $32,657 of that amount from ratepayers. The costs would add about a penny to each customer's electricity bill next year.   Environmentalists say new nets aren't enough. "Once-through" cooling systems, found at more than half of all U.S. reactors, wreak havoc on marine life, they say.  Credit: Dow Jones Newswires

This action follows the capture of a record number of turtles, with some deaths occurring, which could have led to fines under federal endangered species regulations. The utility is actively trying to remove turtles from the canals daily to comply with the U.S. Endangered Species Act, while also facing similar issues at other plants.
moral: Utilities must enhance their efforts to protect endangered species, as current measures like new nets are deemed insufficient by environmentalists.

Title: The 95th Congress: A report card: As historic Congress breaks for halftime, its goal is in sight but remains unmet
Text: Corrections & Amplifications    THE 104TH CONGRESS adjourned for its August recess. A logo accompanying two articles Friday assessing the progress of the present Congress misstated the number.    (WSJ Aug. 14, 1995)   WASHINGTON -- So much begun; so little completed.    That's the status of the Republican campaign to reduce the size and scope of government as senators leave Washington today for their August recess. The remarkable winds of change that propelled Congress full-sail through its first 100 days have continued in the second 100 days, moving beyond the economic issues of the "Contract With America" into a broader range of social, regulatory and budget matters.    Historians say the nation hasn't seen such a burst of congressional activism for more than a century. "What you have on your hands is a quasi prime minister" in House Speaker Newt Gingrich, says Walter Dean Burnham of the University of Texas. "You haven't seen this since Thaddeus Stevens and Reconstruction politics."    In some ways, the pending changes in Washington hardly can be exaggerated. Consider:    -- A year ago, conventional wisdom in both parties claimed balancing the budget would require tax increases as well as spending cuts. Today, the House, Senate and president all have adopted blueprints that balance it with spending cuts alone -- and also pay for tax cuts.    -- A year ago, both parties pushed welfare reform that kept federal control and increased projected spending. Today, the welfare measure that cleared the House, plus that pending in the Senate, would cut spending by tens of billions of dollars and let states run most programs.    -- A year ago, moderate Republicans worked with Democrats to expand minority preferences in government hiring and contracting. Today, Senate Majority Leader Robert Dole advocates eliminating all such preferences.    But for all this commotion, remarkably little of the GOP agenda has actually become law. One central piece -- term limits for members of Congress -- never made it out of the House. Other important bits -- a constitutional amendment to balance the budget, an overhaul of the regulatory process -- are hung up indefinitely in the Senate. And still others -- legal reform, the line-item veto -- have brought deep disagreements between the two bodies and face long odds.    Even the three issues that GOP Chairman Haley Barbour says will determine his party's political prospects next year -- significant progress toward a balanced budget, welfare overhaul and Medicare -- remain far from resolved as the summer recess begins. Sen. Dole's welfare bill was tabled this week because of insufficient support. And GOP leaders remain angst-ridden over their own plans for cutting $270 billion from projected Medicare spending over seven years -- the emotion-laden linchpin of their budget plans.    "If you said back in January that this is where we would be in August, people overall would have been happy," says Timothy Muris, professor of law at George Mason University and an adviser to House Republicans. "But obviously what counts is where we are at Thanksgiving."    And even after the turkey is carved, the revolution's outcome will remain unclear. Hard-edged House Republicans are discovering that their assault on the New Deal and Great Society, which were built over six decades, can't possibly succeed in a single year. Many programs and agencies that Republicans promised to eliminate have only been pruned, raising the possibility they will sprout back with renewed vigor. Balancing the budget will require at least seven years of strict and difficult discipline by congressional appropriations committees and probably a second look at Medicare spending and other entitlement programs after the 1996 election.    As a result, many historians believe that despite talk of parliamentary government, the GOP revolution can't succeed without control of the Executive Branch. "You can't get a cataclysm out of Congress," says Henry Graff, professor emeritus at Columbia University. "The presidency must be won."    Republican leaders are settling in for a long struggle. They're pursuing a strategy to weaken their opponents permanently, cutting off government funds for liberal interest groups and criticizing corporations like Time Warner Inc. that have financed Democrats in the past. GOP coffers are swelling.    But ultimately, continued GOP success will depend on public opinion. And there the jury is out. The latest Wall Street Journal/NBC News poll shows that the number of voters who approve of the job Congress is doing remains higher than before last November's election, but dropped to 36% last month from 47% in April. Possible reasons: Congress's failure to act on term limits, campaign finance and other institutional reforms.    While the verdict is still out on the GOP Congress, historians largely agree that it is in on the president. Unless he wins a second term, Mr. Clinton is well on his way to becoming "an asterisk to history," says Douglas Brinkley, a University of New Orleans historian who is writing a three-volume biography of Jimmy Carter.    Republican leaders emphasize their budget plans don't reduce government spending -- they merely limit its growth. But that understates the dramatic nature of what they have proposed by ignoring the constant pressure put on government spending by inflation and steady population growth.    One useful way of measuring GOP plans is to look at how much of the nation's total output is spent by the federal government. That portion has climbed steadily since the 1930s, reaching 10% in 1940 and climbing to 22% in 1980, which was also the level last year.    If GOP plans are carried out, the government share should drop below 19% in 2002 for the first time since 1966, when President Johnson's Great Society programs began to take hold. But the composition of that spending would be sharply different. Defense then took more than half of every federal dollar; under the GOP plan it will account for only 15% -- leaving more room for costly programs like Medicare and Medicaid. As a result, even if the GOP plan is carried out, it will leave intact major programs put into place in the 1930s and the 1960s. "The heart of the New Deal and the Great Society continues to beat," says biographer Stephen Ambrose.    Congressional appropriations committees, which control roughly a third of the federal budget, face the most difficult task. They must cut their spending from $548 billion this year to $515 billion in 2002. If allowance is made for expected inflation, that cut exceeds 30%.    So far, the House Appropriations Committee has shown surprising discipline, approving bills that cut more than $20 billion in domestic spending authority for the coming year. The Senate is moving more slowly, however, and the president vows to veto many spending bills for cutting too deeply.    One clear flash point will be education. House appropriators cut more than $4 billion from the education budget, and President Clinton is betting that his call to restore some of that money will resonate with the public. An early sign this may give the GOP trouble can be found among Southern and conservative Democrats, who oppose the changes. "Let's stop talking about being too poor to educate our children," Arkansas Democrat Ray Thornton said in an emotional speech to the House Appropriations Committee.    While appropriators have been tough about cutting funds, they have been timid about eliminating whole departments and agencies. The House Appropriations Committee boasts of eliminating in the range of 200 programs. Some, such as energy assistance to the poor and the president's National Service Program, are high-profile. But most are relatively small and obscure, like the Delaware River Basin Commission or the Coast Guard Buoy replacement project. Many high-profile items that were threatened with extinction -- the Commerce Department, the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, the Appalachian Regional Commission -- have survived in shrunken form. That means pressure to revive them all will continue, complicating the task of appropriators who must make even deeper cuts in each of the next six years to meet budget targets.    Meanwhile, the budget proposals also require Congress to pass a welfare overhaul that cuts projected spending on the poor by tens of billions of dollars. And they require projected Medicare cuts totaling $270 billion over seven years.    The Medicare and welfare changes, plus $245 billion of tax cuts over the next five years, are all expected to be in a giant "reconciliation" bill to be acted on this fall. Speaker Gingrich threatens to attach it to a measure increasing the nation's debt limit, forcing President Clinton either to sign the bill or to veto the higher debt limit, possibly triggering an unprecedented default by the U.S. government. The fate of that huge chunk of legislation may become the GOP revolution's most important test.    Lifting the heavy hand of government regulation is a central theme of the Contract With America. And it is high on the agenda of many business groups that helped finance successful GOP campaigns in 1994. But the major effort to slow government regulation by requiring elaborate new cost-benefit analyses was filibustered to death in the Senate.    That hasn't stopped House Republicans from waging war against regulations on numerous other fronts. They have attacked environmental regulations, for instance, by passing one bill to reduce drastically federal protection for wetlands and another to require compensation for people whose property value plummets because of regulatory action. The House also has approved an appropriations bill to cut funds sharply for the Environmental Protection Agency, with 17 "riders" limiting the EPA's ability to enforce environmental laws.    The Senate is sure to weaken many of these House efforts. Yet significant rollback appears inevitable, and administration officials have already begun pre-emptive efforts to revise environmental rules. Anticipating an attack on the Endangered Species Act, for instance, Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt has moved to exempt small landowners from the law.    Labor regulation is another area where House Republicans, spurred by business backers, pursue an aggressive agenda. They have cut funds for agencies like the Occupational Safety and Health Administration and the National Labor Relations Board and attached riders to appropriations bills to limit the agencies' powers. Many of the riders may die in the Senate.    In the end, says Bill Hamilton, director of government relations for the Teamsters union, any change in labor law may be gradual. "You'll feel it over time, but it won't be a lightning flash. It'll be a diminution of regulation, a diminution of safety and a diminution of what we've taken for granted."    While House Republicans have curried favor with some businesses by rolling back labor and environmental regulation, they have taken on others by attacking subsidies for technology development. The House, for instance, voted to stop two leading Clinton plans: Commerce's Advanced Technology Program and the Pentagon's Defense Conversion program. Moreover, they still threaten to eliminate Commerce itself.    Though some big businesses fight for that department and its technology and trade programs, their zeal is muted by approval of other parts of the GOP agenda. Secretary Ron Brown says, "I would never argue that the Department of Commerce, as a name, is more important to corporate America than capital-gains taxes."    One recent and profound change in Washington concerns public policy matters dealing with race. Government affirmative-action programs are under a three-pronged threat -- from a skeptical Supreme Court, a hostile Republican Congress and a public (notably in California) that seems ready to vote against race- and sex-based preferences.    So far, few federal affirmative-action programs have been altered or eliminated. But the trend appears irreversible. "What we can say now is that the civil-rights era is over," says David Bositis, a senior analyst at the liberal Joint Center for Political and Economic Studies.    ---    Bob Davis, David Rogers and Laurie McGinley contributed to this article.    ---                   What Congress Has Done          On the `Contract With America' . . . Title: U.S. regulators sue financier Horowitz over failed thrift
Text: Federal regulators sued financier Charles Hurwitz, seeking damages of at least $250 million for his role in the costly 1988 collapse of a Texas thrift.    Details of the suit, filed in federal court in Houston late yesterday, weren't immediately available. However, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. had said in 1989 that it intended to sue Mr. Hurwitz and certain others for numerous alleged violations of banking laws at United Savings of Texas, a highflying thrift heavily involved in junk bonds, arbitrage and speculative real-estate plays. Mr. Hurwitz owned 23% of United's parent company; United Savings' collapse is expected to cost taxpayers $1.6 billion.    The agency didn't sue at the time because of a then-new policy of trying to negotiate settlements in high-profile thrift cases, but negotiations with Mr. Hurwitz have been at an impasse for several years. Federal regulators and some members of Congress -- not to mention Mr. Hurwitz -- have been increasingly critical of the slow pace of the United Savings case, and the FDIC was under some pressure to either move forward or drop the matter.    Mr. Hurwitz is chairman, chief executive and principal shareholder of Houston-based Maxxam Inc. In a statement issued late yesterday, Richard P. Keeton, Mr. Hurwitz's lawyer, called the FDIC's suit "without merit" and said that "we are outraged that the FDIC has acted in what we believe is an arbitrary and unreasonable manner." Mr. Hurwitz declined to comment.    The United Savings case is one of the last and biggest of the cases from the thrift crisis, but it is of particular interest to many because of its unusual link to the redwood forests of California.    As a result of a controversial 1986 takeover, Mr. Hurwitz and Maxxam own Pacific Lumber Co., the world's biggest producer of redwood lumber. After acquiring the company, Mr. Hurwitz doubled its historic pace of logging. That triggered near-constant legal warfare between conservationists and the company over the fate of the last big privately owned redwood forests.    For several years, environmentalists have been pitching a proposal under which the government would essentially forgive Mr. Hurwitz's alleged liability for United Savings' demise in return for his turning over about 4,000 acres of virgin redwoods known as the Headwaters Forest, which Mr. Hurwitz has been trying to log for years. The concept has support from some influential people, including Vice President Al Gore.    Backers of the idea think the FDIC's move against Mr. Hurwitz may give the plan renewed impetus. "It's past time for a debt-for-nature swap for the Headwaters Forest," said Jill Ratner, an attorney for the Rose Foundation, a backer of the proposal. The FDIC suit "is a real step forward."    Any such deal remains a long shot. For one thing, environmental obstacles to logging the Headwaters Forest could be swept away if Congress waters down the Endangered Species Act; Mr. Hurwitz has been among the act's sternest critics.  Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: Wolves, Spreading West From Idaho, Will Hit Oregon Sooner Than Expected
Text: Gray wolves in Portland? Wildlife officials say it's only a matter of time -- and less time than previously thought. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's reintroduction of the species to Idaho three years ago has proved so successful that officials say the wolves are spreading westward. "They'll be in Oregon in a year or two at the most," says Pete Frost, the National Wildlife Federation's northwest regional director in Portland. "What a challenge for city dwellers, when we suddenly are lower on the food chain." When 35 gray wolves from Canada were released in central Idaho in 1995 and 1996, wildlife biologists figured that if they survived and thrived, they would begin migrating to Oregon and Washington in five to 10 years at the earliest. But in February, a female wolf -- known by her electronic collar number B-45 -- made hash of that schedule by wandering into Oregon, where she spent a month in the Blue Mountains before being captured by federal officials. "We had been thinking we had about five years before we had to think about it," says Rich Berry, wildlife program manager at the Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife. "Then B-45 showed up, and we realized our five years was up." Mr. Berry says the agency is now starting to plan how to educate Oregonians about gray wolves, and how it will respond if wolves are caught killing livestock -- or ranchers are caught killing wolves. It could happen. Ken Holliday, a rancher in John Day, says that he learned earlier this year that B-45 had crossed his property, and decided he would shoot it if it came close to his herd, but he was warned not to by federal authorities, who say ranchers face criminal charges if they kill the wolves. Mr. Holliday says ranchers in his neck of the woods want the federal government to conduct a study to determine whether private property and wild herds of deer, elk and antelope would be able to withstand the return of the gray wolves, which have been extinct in Oregon since 1927. Even without the wolves, Mr. Holliday figures the Endangered Species Act puts more than enough pressure on his livelihood. The John Day River, which runs through his ranch, is home to five species of fish that are either listed as endangered or threatened or are under consideration for listing. "These wolves are just another threat to us," Mr. Holliday says. "There's a reason the wolves aren't here anymore, and that is because when the settlers first came out here they were losing babies on the trail to them." In Washington, gray wolves were wiped out by 1930. Those that have ventured down from Canada since have been shot, says Harriett Allen, manager of the endangered species program at the Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife. "We are certainly going to start working with the people in Southeast Washington" to prepare them for the eventual return of the species, Ms. Allen says. Federal officials -- who have jurisdiction over the wolves because they are protected under the ESA -- believe there are about 110 adult wolves and 60 pups in Idaho now, according to Ed Bangs, the federal Fish and Wildlife Department program manager for wolf reintroduction in the Northwest. Mr. Bangs says that in each pack of wolves, only one pair breeds. The younger wolves either wait for their turn to become a breeder, or leave as yearlings to search for mates and start a new pack. These are the wolves expected to retrace B-45's steps into Oregon, and Mr. Bangs figures there will be as many as 200 candidates for migration by next year. And Mr. Bangs and others say the animals are misunderstood. For instance, they say, there is no proven case of a wolf killing a human. In fact, wolves generally avoid humans. "We need to start educating everybody on what the wolf is and isn't," says Mr. Frost of the National Wildlife Federation. "There is a lot of talk about livestock, but in Montana [where wolves were reintroduced in Yellowstone National Park, also in 1995 and 1996], there are more cattle killed by lightning than by wolves." The federation plans a wolf conference in Portland next month for ranchers, wildlife officials, environmentalists and representatives of Indian tribes. Oregon State Sen. Ted Ferrioli, a Republican from John Day, says education is important -- as is the establishment of state policy. He says the state should decide now "how we are going to deal with the livestock these wolves are going to take, because it's going to happen. "When you introduce large predators, they are going to thin the population of large game," he says. "And that is going to lead them to livestock." Sen. Ferrioli and wolf defenders agree on one thing: All a wolf needs to thrive is the presence of red meat and the absence of humans with guns, which means there's no reason to think that they'll stop once they reach Eastern Oregon. "They'll be across the mountains and down there in Portland before you know it," Sen. Ferrioli says. "And then we'll see who's concerned. Because I hear wolves like poodles. They taste like lamb." (See related letter: "THE WALL STREET JOURNAL / NORTHWEST --- "Letters to the Editor: Canadian Swap" -- WSJ July 7, 1999) Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: The Pickens Plan: Visionary or Blowin' in the Wind?
Text: T. Boone Pickens's letter of Sept. 2 says: "I believe that with private investment and proven technology, we can generate 20% of our electricity from wind within 10 years." No one is stopping him from achieving his goal. He should proceed with his plan. He should buy or lease property, install wind turbines, build transmission lines and sell as much electricity as he can. I just don't want him asking for government subsidies or tax breaks along the way. If he can deliver electricity from wind power more economically than coal, natural gas or nuclear power, he will be rewarded. I don't want the government spending money subsidizing an industry which cannot sustain itself. Nor do I want the government creating artificial demand for natural gas by mandating it be used for transportation. The price of natural gas has risen dramatically in recent years and we don't need to artificially increase the demand for it by using it to fuel cars. We've already seen how government interference in energy markets with ethanol mandates and ethanol subsidies has driven up the price of corn and other food crops. In response to Mr. Pickens's request for a plan, here is my plan. Let the market decide, and don't allow special interests and the government to interfere. When electricity from wind is more economical than other sources, wind will win. Until then, I'd like to keep my electricity, fuel costs and taxes as low as possible. Dan Agan Houston --- The genius of Mr. Pickens's plan is that he is not beating the tired "save the environment" message that so many others have tried to use, and failed, to mobilize America to seek energy alternatives. Let's face it -- Americans don't care that much about the environment. The Pickens Plan is attracting attention because he is saying: America, this is a huge national security issue! His transfer of wealth argument is: Why send $700 billion annually to the Middle East when we should be investing those dollars in domestic energy alternatives? It is not Mr. Pickens's job to be the architect of our country's energy policy going forward. Washington has done nothing over the last 20 years. At least Mr. Pickens is bold enough to lay out the beginning of something constructive, and wealthy enough to mobilize it on his own. Karl Zachar Concord, Mass. --- T. Boone Pickens dares Holman Jenkins to propose a better way than windmills to produce 20% of America's energy needs in 10 years time. I'll accept that challenge. Here is my plan: Nuclear power, which already supplies 20% of our electric power, is a proven technology. So, use the next 10 years to build enough new nuclear plants to match the unproven hopes for substantial energy from windmills. Because those plants can be placed near the energy users they serve, we will not need to spend millions on thousands of miles of long-distance, high-tension lines to move energy from the Great Plains, where Mr. Pickens will build his windmills. Nor will we suffer the losses associated with that transmission. Getting the additional power from nuclear plants also means we can avoid building new plants fueled by natural gas to supply needed power whenever the winds fall short of expectations. To be sure, enriched uranium is not, like wind, a renewable source. We do, however, have plenty of it to meet our needs for a very long time. Think again, Mr. Pickens. James L. Abrahamson Pittsboro, N.C. --- Mr. Pickens's energy plan is incomplete without mention of California's Altamont Pass Wind Farm. During its long lifetime it has killed some 100 eagles and about 1,000 other birds a year. It has been in violation of the Endangered Species Act but seems to enjoy freedom from enforcement. We are a nation of law. Mr. Pickens must address this issue in order to have a plan with meaning. Frank Cotter Ponte Vedra Beach, Fla.

Title: Trump's Next 100 Days to Turn To Tax, Trade and Peace Deals
Text: WASHINGTON -- After a 100-day sprint through domestic priorities, President Trump's focus is shifting abroad, driven by a mountain of trade negotiations with other countries, including China, and unfulfilled promises of attaining peace in Ukraine.By no means is Trump finished at home, where he is consolidating executive power, targeting perceived political enemies, upending the federal bureaucracy, rolling back regulations and imposing strict immigration controls.Advisers said the breakneck start of Trump's second term had made room for other aspects of his packed agenda.White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said Trump had made progress on his twin goals of securing the border and steadying the economy. "The next 100 days will consist of trade deals, peace deals and tax cuts," she said. "More American greatness is on the way."That confidence will be tested.Trump's far-reaching tariffs have strained relations with allies. He is growing impatient with the pace of talks to end the war in Ukraine. His plans to rebuild Gaza have stalled as fighting between Israel and Hamas continues. He has launched a trade war with China. And he is threatening military action against Iran if talks to limit the country's nuclear program collapse."You're in the disruption phase right now," said former House Speaker Kevin McCarthy, a California Republican. "He's reshaped the power structure. People don't really look to the House or the Senate anymore. They look to the executive branch."In May, the president plans to visit Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, and he plans to travel later this year to the U.K. for a state visit. Last week, Trump accepted an invitation to meet with Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni of Italy "in the very near future."He is also, according to a senior adviser, hoping to make progress on his ambitions for territorial expansion, setting his sights on Greenland and the Panama Canal.Trump, a Republican, enters the new phase with growing consumer and business concerns over tariffs and sagging polling numbers, though his standing among core Republicans remains firm. Internal policy disagreements and personality clashes have begun to surface, and Trump's habit of shifting gears has Democrats feeling better about their prospects."I fully expect there will be 100 days more of chaos and confusion," said Rep. Brendan Boyle (D., Pa.). Democratic pollster Douglas Schoen said, "Even though my party is disoriented, divided, without a strategy or a message, Democrats can win a midterm just by being the opposition."Tariff negotiationsTrade will continue to dominate Trump's agenda, following the president's decision early this month to impose tariffs on dozens of countries. A 90-day pause on some tariffs on all nations except China opened the door for negotiations that in the coming weeks and months will test the stamina of a Trump team trying to deliver wins for a president who says his goal is to reorder global trade.The administration is planning additional measures to expand the mining of critical minerals used in defense, energy and other industries, according to advisers, an attempt to offset the reliance on China and other countries. Trump has also championed a spate of private-sector investments in the U.S. since his election, and the White House is planning additional announcements.Trump has grown increasingly frustrated over the lack of progress in ending the war in Ukraine, according to people close to him, raising the prospect that he could leave the two warring countries to continue fighting while the U.S. focuses on other priorities such as trade and the Iran nuclear talks.More ordersDespite growing demands abroad, much of Trump's focus remains at home.White House officials said the president is expected to continue signing executive orders each week, with an increasing focus on deregulation.Agencies also are working on rules to entrench conservative policies, including one that would make it easier for industries to get around Endangered Species Act impediments that slow infrastructure development.The administration is also discussing new policy proposals to grow pharmaceutical production in the U.S., advisers said.Though Elon Musk is preparing to limit his role overseeing the effort that has slashed tens of thousands of federal jobs, the Department of Government Efficiency will continue its work, officials said. The overall DOGE program has fallen significantly short of cost-saving claims.On Capitol Hill, Trump's chief legislative priority is taking shape and could become law this spring or summer. Republicans unlocked a procedural fast track for a bill that would extend expiring tax cuts, lower taxes further and increase spending for border security and national defense. The border money would help fund what the administration said will be a more aggressive effort to deport people living in the U.S. illegally, steps that could include more workplace raids.Trump also is planning to unveil a plan to offer cash incentives to people in the country illegally who self-deport, a senior adviser said. The administration is completing a proposal to restrict travel to the U.S. from certain countries, reviving limits put in place during Trump's first term. The administration could also unveil agreements with countries to take migrants deported from the U.S. The administration has been in conversations with countries in Africa, Asia and Eastern Europe, officials said."Your first year is likely your opportunity to get most of your legislative accomplishments done in our new partisan world," said Marc Short, Trump's first-term legislative affairs director. But Short said passing any bill wouldn't be easy. "It does seem like there's been a lot of political capital wasted on a trade war."Midterms aheadThe president plans to mark the end of his first 100 days and look forward to 2026 with a rally Tuesday in the battleground state of Michigan. Trump flipped the state in 2024, and Republicans are expected to try to topple the Democrat-held Senate seat there next year. While Republicans hold the Senate and have a slim majority in the House, the president's party traditionally loses ground in the midterm elections.Trump has raised millions of dollars for his political-action committee and the Republican Party, and he is starting to dole out endorsements. But hanging over the midterm elections will be Trump's handling of the economy, and Republicans have warned that if trade deals aren't accomplished in the next year -- and the markets don't settle -- they will face political headwinds.Even as Democrats struggle to regroup after the 2024 election, they are coalescing around public backlash to Musk, DOGE and the impact of Trump's trade wars at home."I believe he has from now to about January 1 to be very disruptive," said former House Speaker Newt Gingrich, a Republican and a Trump ally. After that, he said, Trump "needs to be stabilizing, pulling together and explaining."By Alex Leary and Meridith McGraw

Title: Preserving Threatened Species, Even Property Owners
Text: In response to your March 11 editorial "Fishing for Wildlife Lawsuits," I'd like to provide a reality check. First, let's start with numbers. The U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service settled more Endangered Species Act lawsuits during the Bush administration than the current administration. The "sue and settle" assertion is simply wrong. The ESA requires us, under tight deadlines, to evaluate imperiled species and protect those facing extinction. We're an equal-opportunity defendant when we miss those deadlines, sued by development and environmental groups alike. By establishing agreement with our most frequent litigants on a schedule for listing decisions, the 2011 settlements reduce lawsuits, provide predictability for stakeholders and allow us to focus on species that evidence suggests face the greatest extinction risk. Our decisions are always made transparently, incorporating robust public involvement and independent scientific peer review. This settlement requires us to make decisions, not list species. For example, we determined that the dunes sagebrush lizard doesn't require ESA protection due to voluntary conservation commitments made in New Mexico and Texas by federal, state and private landowners -- including the oil and gas industry. The settlement gives 11 Western states, under the bipartisan leadership of Govs. Matt Mead (R., Wyo.) and John Hickenlooper (D., Colo.), until 2015 to work with stakeholders to conserve the greater sage-grouse, possibly avoiding the need for ESA protection. Last year, a federal judge cited the settlement in upholding that date, providing time to implement effective conservation measures that work best for local communities. You may disagree with the law. But this debate should be steeped in facts. Dan Ashe Director U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service Washington --- Your indictment of the enforcement of the Endangered Species Act is considerably understated. The federal government using the extended powers assumed under the Clean Water Act to create "central planning" coupled with the ESA has in many states resulted in a complete abrogation of the theory of the rights associated with private property ownership. When the additional impact of effective extortion associated with the doling out of federal transportation dollars is added to the "planning" effort, private property exists only in the mind of the tax collector. In Washington state, under a Growth Management Act passed over the objection voiced in a citizens' ballot initiative, each county must centrally plan and identify "critical areas" for protection. In Kitsap County, where I live, approximately 22% of all private property is encumbered by "critical area" buffers or restrictions that preclude entry or use by property owners who must still pay taxes at the "highest and best use" rate. In addition, the county with over 500 miles of shoreline has a Shoreline Management Plan (a different name for critical-area protection) that encumbers the first 50 to 100 feet of property from the high-water mark. Many shoreline plots are only 100 feet deep. To further exacerbate the situation, the county has a unique application of the "nonconforming use" law that effectively prevents future use of an encumbered property. A precondition for receipt of federal transportation funds is effective compliance with GMA and ESA. Perhaps the single most endangered of species in Kitsap County is the private property owner. Jack Hamilton Silverdale, Wash. Subscribe to WSJ:

Title: Lobbyists' Smelt-and-Bird Campaign Is Assault against Endangered Species Act Itself, Some Say
Text: Some federal scientists fear that politics is starting to overwhelm science in the growing debate over the impact of the Endangered Species Act on economic development.    Faced with an extraordinary lobbying campaign by businessmen and politicians, the Fish and Wildlife Service has taken the unusual step of watering down the findings of its own field scientists that a tiny California fish, the delta smelt, is heading for extinction and should be listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act. The service now is weighing whether to recommend listing the smelt as a threatened species, a lower-priority category under the act that gets significantly less protection than an endangered species. Some federal scientists involved in the case believe that the threatened status, even if granted by the agency, isn't enough to prevent the smelt from being exterminated within two or three years.    Federal scientists also say the service is considering similarly overruling or diluting recommendations of scientists that a small songbird, the California coastal gnatcatcher, be granted endangered-species status as well. A final decision on the smelt had been due June 29 and now may come any day. The gnatcatcher ruling is scheduled for next month.    Such altering of staff recommendations is relatively rare. Under certain circumstances, it can be illegal: The Endangered Species Act requires that only scientific data about the health of a species -- not economic, social or political considerations -- figure into whether a species is granted endangered-species status.    There's nothing illegal about going to Congress to argue openly that water, housing or other human needs are more important than the fate of some animals. Indeed, that issue is the core of the escalating debate over whether the Endangered Species Act should be revised; the act is up for reauthorization next year, in what now promises to be a bloody political brawl between environmentalists who have used the act to restrain growth and business interests who think wildlife preservation is going too far.    But in the California cases, contend scientists familiar with them, business interests, politicians and some top-level bureaucrats are engaging in a backroom end run around established procedures and law. They assert that Fish and Wildlife brass are wavering on protecting the two animals because of a lobbying blitz from well-connected California real-estate and agricultural companies, with an unusual behind-the-scenes boost from California state politicians and the staffs of such administration figures as Vice President Quayle. The companies have been galvanized by the belief that ensuring the survival of smelt and gnatcatchers would have far-reaching and costly implications for water, agriculture and land development in California.    "Political science, and not biological science, is determining the fate of these species," says Felix Smith, a recently retired biologist with the service's Sacramento, Calif., office who is familiar with both studies. Another federal scientist who worked on one of the studies adds that the alleged political influence "is frustrating, and it is not supposed to be permitted under the law."    Both the White House and the Interior Department, of which the Fish and Wildlife Service is an arm, deny that any unusual influence is being leveled against listing the animals. Mr. Quayle's office acknowledges that a staff member attended an Interior Department meeting regarding the gnatcatcher, but adds that the staffer didn't make any comments during the proceeding. "We have weighed in not at all," says David Beckwith, Mr. Quayle's press secretary.    However, some federal scientists and veteran environmental lobbyists describe as unusual any contact between administration staff and wildlife officials over a species under consideration for listing as endangered; they say that is a form of pressure in itself. "What we're seeing here is the beginning of an attack, not on delta smelt or California gnatcatchers, but on the Endangered Species Act itself," says William Davoren, founder of the Bay Institute, a Sausilito, Calif., environmental group.    Federal scientists involved in both the smelt and gnatcatcher cases say they can recall few other instances in which agency higher-ups rejected recommendations on protecting a species. One was in the mid-1980s, when the service, under pressure from Northwest timber interests, doctored early staff studies to play down indications that the spotted owl was in trouble. The General Accounting Office and two federal judges later cited that action as an apparent violation of the Endangered Species Act.    Environmental groups frequently accuse wildlife agencies of similar acts, but in this case, several of the agency's own scientists have leveled the charge. Bob Walker, an Interior Department spokesman, says, "No one {from California or representing smelt and gnatcatcher opponents} met with anyone who is on the team working out the final decisions" or tried to exert any unusual influence. There is evidence suggesting otherwise.    Exhibit A, say some federal scientists, is the smelt study. The minnow-like creatures live only in the delta system formed as the Sacramento and San Joaquin rivers flow into San Francisco Bay. After a year of study, biologists with the Fish and Wildlife Service's Sacramento office concluded that the smelt population had plunged to about 200,000 from two million in the 1970s and could be extinct within a few years. Regional headquarters recommended that the smelt be listed as endangered.    Normally, such dire staff findings are expeditiously approved by Fish and Wildlife brass back in Washington. But the smelt report languished as lobbying groups representing powerful farm interests and water agencies fanned out over Washington. Those interests would be hurt by a listing, because protecting smelt would almost certainly sharply reduce the amount of water that could be drawn from the delta and pumped southward, particularly for irrigation. The huge pumps suck in and mince tens of thousands of smelt annually.    Douglas Wheeler and Michael Mantell, director and deputy director, respectively, of California's Department of Resources, acknowledge that they met in Washington with Richard Smith and other Interior Department officials to discuss, among other things, concerns about the impact of protecting the smelt on the state's water system. Mr. Smith, a deputy director of the Fish and Wildlife Service, is directly responsible for overseeing the smelt and gnatcatcher studies. (The Californians say they're neutral on the two species, and merely met with agency officials to keep them informed of various state environmental issues.)    Earlier this month, six weeks after the original deadline for ruling on the staff findings, Mr. Smith kicked the smelt report back to the service's Western regional headquarters in Portland, Ore., instructing officials there to lower their recommendation to threatened from endangered. For the smelt, the distinction could be crucial, because threatened status would allow continued operation of the smelt-killing pumps, while endangered status would halt pumping or require other drastic steps to avoid killing smelt.    In a rare show of bureaucratic defiance, the service's Sacramento scientists refused to participate in the re-evaluation of their original findings. But last week, the service's regional office sent back a revised recommendation: Threatened.    Mr. Smith says he based his decision purely on his review of the scientific data, which he believes don't warrant listing the smelt as endangered at this time. He characterizes the lobbying around the smelt issue as heavier than in most proposed listings, but says that hasn't influenced the agency's actions. "Political pressure has not been a factor," he says. But several federal scientists don't buy that: "It is sad to see the agency prove so vulnerable to outside pressure," says one. As for the smelt, many biologists, inside and outside the government, don't think threatened status will be enough to prevent its extinction.    The agency is waffling on the gnatcatcher, the scientists assert, because of similar high-powered lobbying. The four-inch songbird lives in the so-called "coastal sage scrub" that borders the Southern California coast. Some federal scientists fear that it could be exterminated because its habitat is rapidly being bulldozed under to make way for housing tracts. The Fish and Wildlife Service believes there are only about 2,000 pairs of coastal gnatcatchers left in the U.S. California wildlife officials are also considering listing the gnatcatcher as endangered under state environmental laws.    Much of what remains of the gnatcatcher's habitat is owned by Southern California real estate concerns such as Irvine Cos., Baldwin Co. and Santa Margarita Co., which are among the nation's biggest developers and Republican campaign contributors. Hank Hankla, a Washington lawyer heading up their lobbying campaign against listing the gnatcatchers, says his group has spent nearly $1 million in the last year to refute scientific data indicating that the gnatcatcher should be listed as endangered.    Mr. Hankla says his group has argued its case in audiences with everyone from Interior Secretary Manuel Lujan to staff members of Mr. Quayle's Council on Competitiveness. The developers' position also got a nudge from Messrs. Wheeler and Mantell, the California officials; they believe that listing the bird might torpedo an embryonic state plan for protecting coastal habitat that depends on the cooperation of developers.    A federal official says the agency was initially prepared to move fast on the gnatcatcher study because of fears that some of the developers might try to plow under as much of their coastal habitat as possible before any protections go into effect. He says top agency officials were ready to sign off on the gnatcatcher recommendation until the meetings with Messrs. Wheeler and Mantell. "Now, it's in limbo land," says the official.  Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal

Title: Senate should act on biodiversity, U.S. official says
Text: WASHINGTON -- The U.S. may be unable to check protectionist moves by developing countries if the Senate doesn't quickly ratify the biodiversity treaty, a senior Clinton administration official said.    Tim Wirth, undersecretary of state for global affairs, told reporters that inaction by the Senate on the international species-protection treaty would keep the U.S. from participating in a crucial meeting of the treaty's signatories set for November. At the meeting, Mr. Wirth said, developing nations are expected to advocate "very protectionist protocols" that could limit U.S. access to materials used to develop new varieties of crops and biotechnically derived pharmaceuticals. That could hurt U.S. exports of biotech products, he warned.    "If we have not ratified the treaty, we're not sitting at the table," Mr. Wirth said. Although the U.S. could still attend the November meeting as an observer, he said, it would have considerably less influence on the outcome.    The biodiversity treaty, a product of the 1992 Earth Summit, is aimed at protecting plant and animal species around the world; of particular interest to U.S. companies are rare-plant species in tropical climates that may have medicinal, agricultural or industrial value. President Bush refused to sign the treaty on the ground that it would undermine U.S. biotech patent rights, but President Clinton agreed to sign it after drawing up interpretive language that the administration says will protect U.S. patents.    The treaty generated little controversy when it came before the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. But the Cattlemen's Association, a trade group representing U.S. ranchers, has opposed it on the grounds that it would inhibit efforts in the U.S. to scale back the Endangered Species Act. Senate Republicans, including minority leader Bob Dole of Kansas, have seized on this opposition to block ratification on the Senate floor. Mr. Wirth said the treaty would have no effect on any efforts to revise the endangered-species law.  Credit: Staff Reporter of The Wall Street Journal
